***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange.\"[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: See also\")]\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Wheeler 2003 p. 273\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-2)** Wheeler 2003 pp. 273–274\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Milton 1953 p. 871\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-1) Wheeler 2003 p. 274\\n5. **[^](#cite_ref-5)** Milton 1953 p. 874\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** Milton 1953 p. 890\\n7. **[^](#cite_ref-7)** Keeble 2003 p. 132\\n8. **[^](#cite_ref-8)** Stevens 1988 p. 268\\n9. **[^](#cite_ref-9)** Wheeler 2003 p. 275\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n* Keeble, N. [g]\")\\n\\nAppearance\\n\\nmove to sidebar\\nhide\\n\\nFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\\n\\nGroup of clergy active in 1641 England\\n\\n**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name \"Pen name\")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan \"Puritan\") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England \"England\") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland \"Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland\"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) \"Thomas Young (1587-1655)\")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.\\n\\nThe name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) \"Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)\"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder \"Edmund Calamy the Elder\"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen \"Matthew Newcomen\"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow \"William Spurstow\"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall\\'s](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton \"John Milton\") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus\\'s reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThis response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. **Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").

Works
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Works")]

* [A defence of infant-baptism in answer to two treatises](//archive.org/details/defenceofinfantb00mars "iarchive:defenceofinfantb00mars")

He worked as a contributor on:

* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus") (contributor)
* [Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Shorter_Catechism "Shorter Catechism") (contributor)

### Sermons

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Sermons")]

* [A sermon Preached before the Honourable House of Commons, now assembled in Parliament](//archive.org/details/asermonpreached00marsgoog "iarchive:asermonpreached00marsgoog"), at their publike Fast, 17 November 1640. Upon 2 Chron. 15. 2 (1641)
* [The Song of Moses, the Servant of God, and the Song of the Lamb](//archive.org/details/songmosesservan00commgoog "iarchive:songmosesservan00commgoog")(1643)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").

Final antiprelatical tract by John Milton

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. [g]\")\\n\\nAppearance\\n\\nmove to sidebar\\nhide\\n\\nFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\\n\\nGroup of clergy active in 1641 England\\n\\n**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name \"Pen name\")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan \"Puritan\") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England \"England\") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland \"Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland\"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) \"Thomas Young (1587-1655)\")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.\\n\\nThe name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) \"Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)\"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder \"Edmund Calamy the Elder\"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen \"Matthew Newcomen\"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow \"William Spurstow\"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall\\'s](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton \"John Milton\") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus\\'s reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThis response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.\\n\\nMilton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions \"Animadversions\")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus \"Apology for Smectymnuus\")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Hoover, David L.; Corns, Thomas N. Please help to [improve](/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Reliability \"Wikipedia:WikiProject Reliability\") this article by [introducing](/wiki/Wikipedia:When_to_cite \"Wikipedia:When to cite\") more precise citations. *(February 2012)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal \"Help:Maintenance template removal\"))* |  *([Learn how and when to remove this message](/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal \"Help:Maintenance template removal\"))* |\\n\\n**Stephen Marshall** (c.\\u20091594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England \"England\") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) \"Nonconformist (Protestantism)\") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym \"John Pym\") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only \"systematic\" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism \"Infant Baptism\")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes \"John Tombes\") (1646).\\n\\nEarly life\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Early life\")]\\n\\nHe was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester \"Godmanchester\") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire \"Huntingdonshire\"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge \"Emmanuel College, Cambridge\") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex \"Wethersfield, Essex\") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England \"Essex, England\"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield \"Finchingfield\"). In 1636 he was reported for \"want of conformity.\"\\n\\nCivil War years\\n---------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Civil War years\")]\\n\\nMarshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie \"Robert Baillie\") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament \"Short Parliament\") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon \"Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon\") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud \"William Laud\") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret\\'s, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster \"St. Margaret\\'s, Westminster\"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.\\n\\nHe had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex\\'s regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment \"Earl of Essex\\'s regiment\") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland \"Scotland\") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference \"Uxbridge Conference\") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter\\'s execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House \"Holmby House\") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle \"Carisbrooke Castle\").\\n\\nLater life\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Later life\")]\\n\\nA moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian \"Presbyterian\"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism \"Westminster Shorter Catechism\") in 1647, and was one of the \"Triers\" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey \"Westminster Abbey\"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration \"English Restoration\").\\n\\nWorks\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: Works\")]\\n\\n* [A defence of infant-baptism in answer to two treatises](//archive.org/details/defenceofinfantb00mars \"iarchive:defenceofinfantb00mars\")\\n\\nHe worked as a contributor on:\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\") (contributor)\\n* [Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Shorter_Catechism \"Shorter Catechism\") (contributor)\\n\\n### Sermons\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Sermons\")]\\n\\n* [A sermon Preached before the Honourable House of Commons, now assembled in Parliament](//archive.org/details/asermonpreached00marsgoog \"iarchive:asermonpreached00marsgoog\"), at their publike Fast, 17 November 1640.
