It was as a prolific scholar and writer that Selden won his reputation. The early books were on English history.

### English history and antiquities

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: English history and antiquities")]

In 1610 three of his works came out: *Jani Anglorum Facies Altera* (*The Back Face* [or *Two Faces*] *of the English [Janus](/wiki/Janus "Janus")*) and *England's Epinomis*,[[16]](#cite_note-16) which dealt with the progress of English law down to [Henry II](/wiki/Henry_II_of_England "Henry II of England"); and *The Duello, or Single Combat*, in which he traced the history of [trial by battle](/wiki/Trial_by_combat "Trial by combat") in England from the Norman Conquest. In 1613 he supplied a series of notes, including quotations and references, to the first eighteen [cantos](/wiki/Canto "Canto") of [Michael Drayton](/wiki/Michael_Drayton "Michael Drayton")'s *[Poly-Olbion](/wiki/Poly-Olbion "Poly-Olbion")*. In 1614 he published *Titles of Honor*,[[17]](#cite_note-17) which, in spite of defects and omissions, remained a comprehensive work for centuries.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7) It was republished in a larger and greatly revised edition in 1631, and in a third edition in 1672. It earned for Selden the praise "monarch of letters" from his friend [Ben Jonson](/wiki/Ben_Jonson "Ben Jonson").[[18]](#cite_note-18)

In 1615, the *Analecton Anglobritannicon*, an account of the civil administration of England before the [Norman Conquest](/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest"), written in 1607, was published; its title and argument imitated the *[Franco-Gallia](/wiki/Franco-Gallia "Franco-Gallia")* of [François Hotman](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hotman "François Hotman").[[19]](#cite_note-19) In 1616 appeared notes on [John Fortescue](/wiki/John_Fortescue_(judge) "John Fortescue (judge)")'s *De laudibus legum Angliae* and [Ralph de Hengham](/wiki/Ralph_de_Hengham "Ralph de Hengham")'s *Summae magna et parva*.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In 1618 his controversial *History of Tithes* was published. A first sign of the coming storm was the 1619 book controverting Selden, *Sacrilege Sacredly Handled in two parts; with an Appendix, answering some objections* by [James Sempill](/wiki/James_Sempill "James Sempill").[[21]](#cite_note-21) Selden hit back, but was soon gagged. The churchmen [Richard Tillesley](/wiki/Richard_Tillesley "Richard Tillesley") (1582–1621) (*Animadversions upon M. Seldens History of Tithes*, 1619) and [Richard Montagu](/wiki/Richard_Montagu "Richard Montagu") (*Diatribae upon the first part of the late History of Tithes*, 1621) attacked the work.[[22]](#cite_note-22) There were further replies by [William Sclater](/wiki/William_Sclater_(priest) "William Sclater (priest)") (*The Quaestion of Tythes Revised*, 1623), and by [Stephen Nettles](/wiki/Stephen_Nettles "Stephen Nettles") (*Answer to the Jewish Part of Mr. Selden's History of Tithes* 1625). In it Selden tried to demonstrate that tithing depended on the civil law, rather than [canon law](/wiki/Canon_law "Canon law"). He also made much of the complexities of the ancient Jewish customs on tithes.[[23]](#cite_note-23)
The work was also a milestone in the history of English historical writing through its mixture of [antiquarian](/wiki/Antiquarian "Antiquarian")-philological scholarship with historical narrative, two approaches to the study of the past previously seen as distinct.

In 1623 he produced an edition of [Eadmer](/wiki/Eadmer "Eadmer")'s *Historia Novarum*. It was notable for including in appendices information from the *[Domesday Book](/wiki/Domesday_Book "Domesday Book")*, which at the time had not been published and could only be consulted in the original at Westminster, on the payment of a fee.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

He published in 1642 *Privileges of the Baronage of England when they sit in Parliament and Discourse concerning the Rights and Privileges of the Subject*. In 1652 he wrote a preface and collated some of the manuscripts for [Sir Roger Twysden's](/wiki/Roger_Twysden "Roger Twysden") *Historiae Anglicanae scriptores X*.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/John_Selden%2C_Tracts_Written_by_John_Selden_of_the_Inner-Temple%2C_Esquire_%281st_ed%2C_1683%2C_title_page%29.jpg/250px-John_Selden%2C_Tracts_Written_by_John_Selden_of_the_Inner-Temple%2C_Esquire_%281st_ed%2C_1683%2C_title_page%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Selden,_Tracts_Written_by_John_Selden_of_the_Inner-Temple,_Esquire_(1st_ed,_1683,_title_page).jpg)

*Tracts*, published posthumously in 1683, contained English translations

### Literature and archaeology of the Near East

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Literature and archaeology of the Near East")]

In 1617, his *De dis Syris* was issued, and immediately established his fame as an orientalist. It is remarkable for its early use of the comparative method, on [Semitic mythology](/wiki/Semitic_mythology "Semitic mythology").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7) Also, in 1642, he published a part of the Arabic chronicle of [Patriarch Eutychius of Alexandria](/wiki/Patriarch_Eutychius_of_Alexandria "Patriarch Eutychius of Alexandria"), under the title *Eutychii Aegyptii, Patriarchae Orthodoxorum Alexandrini, ... ecclesiae suae origines*. Controversial was the discussion in it of the absence in Alexandria of the distinction between priests and bishops, a burning issue in the debate at the time in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").[[25]](#cite_note-25)

In 1628, at the suggestion of Sir Robert Cotton, Selden compiled, with the assistance of two other scholars, [Patrick Young](/wiki/Patrick_Young "Patrick Young") and [Richard James](/wiki/Richard_James_(scholar) "Richard James (scholar)"), a catalogue of the [Arundel marbles](/wiki/Arundel_marbles "Arundel marbles").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)

### Studies on Judaism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Studies on Judaism")]

He employed his leisure at Wrest in writing *De successionibus in bona defuncti secundum leges Ebraeorum* and *De successione in pontificatum Ebraeorum*, published in 1631.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)

During the progress of the constitutional conflict, he was absorbed in research, publishing *De jure naturali et gentium juxta disciplinam Ebraeorum* in 1640.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600–601-26) It was a contribution to the theorising of the period on [natural law](/wiki/Natural_law "Natural law"). In the words of [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton"), this "volume of naturall & national laws proves, not only by great authorities brought together, but by exquisite reasons and theorems almost mathematically demonstrative, that all opinions, yea errors, known, read, and collated, are of main service & assistance toward the speedy attainment of what is truest."[[4]](#cite_note-naturall-4)[[27]](#cite_note-27) It develops into a theory of [international law](/wiki/International_law "International law"), taking as its basis the [Seven Laws of Noah](/wiki/Seven_Laws_of_Noah "Seven Laws of Noah").[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In 1644, he published *Dissertatio de anno civili et calendario reipublicae Judaicae*, in 1646 his treatise on marriage and divorce among the Jews entitled *Uxor Ebraica*, and in 1647 the earliest printed edition of the old English law-book *[Fleta](/wiki/Fleta "Fleta")*. In 1650 Selden began to print the trilogy he planned on the [Sanhedrin](/wiki/Sanhedrin "Sanhedrin"), as the first part of *De synedriis et prefecturis juridicis veterum Ebraeorum* through the press, the second and third parts being severally published in 1653 and 1655.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9) The aim of this work was to counter the use by the Presbyterians, in particular, of arguments and precedents drawn from Jewish tradition; it was a very detailed study aimed at refuting such arguments, and pointing out the inherent flexibility of the tradition that was being cited.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

### International law

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: International law")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/John_Selden_from_NPG_%282%29_cleaned.jpg/250px-John_Selden_from_NPG_%282%29_cleaned.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Selden_from_NPG_(2)_cleaned.jpg)

A portrait of John Selden held by the [National Portrait Gallery, London](/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery,_London "National Portrait Gallery, London")

His *[Mare clausum](/wiki/Mare_clausum "Mare clausum")* was written to dismantle the pretensions advanced by [Grotius](/wiki/Hugo_Grotius "Hugo Grotius") in *[The Free Sea](/wiki/The_Free_Sea "The Free Sea")* (*Mare liberum*), on behalf of the Dutch fishermen, to poach in the waters off the English coasts.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)

The circumstances of its delayed publication, in 1635, suggest that during the early 1630s Selden inclined towards the court rather than the popular party and even secured the personal favour of the king, [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"). It had been written sixteen or seventeen years earlier, but for political reasons Charles's predecessor, [James I](/wiki/James_I_of_England "James I of England"), had prohibited its publication. When it eventually appeared, a quarter of a century after *Mare liberum*, it was under Charles's royal patronage, as a kind of state paper, and with a dedication to him. The fact that Selden was not retained in the great case of [ship money](/wiki/Ship_money "Ship money") in 1637 by [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden "John Hampden"), the cousin of Sir Edmund, his former client in the Five Knights' Case, may be taken as additional evidence that his zeal for the popular cause was neither so warm nor so unquestioned as it had once been.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)

His last publication was a vindication of himself from certain charges advanced against him and his *Mare clausum* around 1653 by [Theodore Graswinckel](/wiki/Theodore_Graswinckel "Theodore Graswinckel"), a Dutch jurist.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9)

### Posthumous publications

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Posthumous publications")]

Several of Selden's minor works were printed for the first time after his death, including a tract in defence of the 25 December birth of Christ written during the Puritan Commonwealth (1649–1660) when celebration of Christmas was prohibited.[[30]](#cite_note-30) A collective edition of his writings was published by [David Wilkins](/wiki/David_Wilkins_(archdeacon) "David Wilkins (archdeacon)") in 3 volumes folio in 1725, and again in 1726. *Table Talk*, for which he is perhaps best known, did not appear until 1689. It was edited by his [amanuensis](/wiki/Amanuensis "Amanuensis"), [Richard Milward](/wiki/Richard_Milward_(priest) "Richard Milward (priest)"), who affirms that "the sense and notion is wholly Selden's" and that "most of the words" are his also. Its genuineness has sometimes been questioned.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9)

Views
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Views")]

Selden arrived at an [Erastian](/wiki/Erastian "Erastian") position in church politics. He also believed in [free will](/wiki/Free_will "Free will"), which was inconsistent with [Calvinism](/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism").[[31]](#cite_note-31)

He was sceptical of the legend of [King Arthur](/wiki/King_Arthur "King Arthur") as it had grown up, but believed Arthur had existed.[[32]](#cite_note-32) The [Druids](/wiki/Druids "Druids"), he suggested in comments on *Poly-Olbion*, were ancient and presumed esoteric thinkers.[[33]](#cite_note-33) The popular image of a Druid descends via a masque of [Inigo Jones](/wiki/Inigo_Jones "Inigo Jones") from a reconstruction by Selden, based (without good foundations) on ancient German statuary.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

Commemoration
-------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Commemoration")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Selden_Soc_vols.jpg/500px-Selden_Soc_vols.jpg)](/wiki/File:Selden_Soc_vols.jpg)

Volumes published by the [Selden Society](/wiki/Selden_Society "Selden Society")

Selden is commemorated in the name of the [Selden Society](/wiki/Selden_Society "Selden Society"), a [learned society](/wiki/Learned_society "Learned society") concerned with the study of English legal history, founded in 1887.

He is also commemorated in place-names in Salvington, including "The John Selden Inn", which purports to be on the site of his dwelling; Selden Road; and the Selden medical centre. Also The Selden Arms on Lyndhurst Road in Worthing.

Influence
---------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Influence")]

According to the *Encyclopedia of Historians and Historical Writing*, he "played a role of fundamental importance in the transition of English historical writing from a medieval antiquarianism to a more modern understanding of the scope and function of history than had ever before been expressed in Renaissance England".[[35]](#cite_note-35) His reputation lasted well, with [Mark Pattison](/wiki/Mark_Pattison_(academic) "Mark Pattison (academic)") calling him "the most learned man, not only of his party, but of Englishmen".[[36]](#cite_note-36)

By about 1640, Selden's views (with those of Grotius) had a large impact on the [Great Tew circle](/wiki/Great_Tew_circle "Great Tew circle") around [Lucius Cary, 2nd Viscount Falkland](/wiki/Lucius_Cary,_2nd_Viscount_Falkland "Lucius Cary, 2nd Viscount Falkland"): [William Chillingworth](/wiki/William_Chillingworth "William Chillingworth"), [Dudley Digges](/wiki/Dudley_Digges "Dudley Digges"), [Henry Hammond](/wiki/Henry_Hammond "Henry Hammond").[[37]](#cite_note-37) It was in this milieu that Selden met and befriended [Thomas Hobbes](/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes "Thomas Hobbes"). They had much in common, in political thought, but the precise connections have not been clarified.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

[Richard Cumberland](/wiki/Richard_Cumberland_(philosopher) "Richard Cumberland (philosopher)") followed Selden over both Grotius and Hobbes on natural law. Selden contested the scholastic position, after [Cicero](/wiki/Cicero "Cicero"), that "right reason" could by its dictates alone generate [obligation](/wiki/Moral_obligation "Moral obligation"), by claiming that a formal obligation required a superior in authority. In his *De legibus* Cumberland rejects Selden's solution by means of the Noahide laws, in *De jure naturali*, in favour of Selden's less developed alternate solution. The latter is more orthodox for a [Thomist](/wiki/Thomist "Thomist"), an *intellectus agens* as a natural faculty in the rational soul, by the mediation of which divine intellect can intervene directly with individuals.[[39]](#cite_note-39) [Matthew Hale](/wiki/Matthew_Hale_(jurist) "Matthew Hale (jurist)") tried to merge the theory of Grotius on property with Selden's view on obligation.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Cumberland and Hale both belonged to a larger group, followers in a broad sense of Selden, with backgrounds mostly of Cambridge and the law, comprising also [Orlando Bridgeman](/wiki/Sir_Orlando_Bridgeman,_1st_Baronet,_of_Great_Lever "Sir Orlando Bridgeman, 1st Baronet, of Great Lever"), [Hezekiah Burton](/wiki/Hezekiah_Burton "Hezekiah Burton"), [John Hollings](/wiki/John_Hollings "John Hollings"), [Richard Kidder](/wiki/Richard_Kidder "Richard Kidder"), [Edward Stillingfleet](/wiki/Edward_Stillingfleet "Edward Stillingfleet"), [John Tillotson](/wiki/John_Tillotson "John Tillotson"), and [John Wilkins](/wiki/John_Wilkins "John Wilkins").[[41]](#cite_note-41)

[Giambattista Vico](/wiki/Giambattista_Vico "Giambattista Vico") called Grotius, Selden and [Samuel Pufendorf](/wiki/Samuel_Pufendorf "Samuel Pufendorf") the "three princes" of the "natural right of the gentes". He went on to criticise their approach foundationally.[[42]](#cite_note-42) In his *Autobiography* he specifies that they had conflated the natural law of the "nations", based on custom, with that of the philosophers, based on human abstractions.[[43]](#cite_note-43) [Isaiah Berlin](/wiki/Isaiah_Berlin "Isaiah Berlin") comments on Vico's admiration for Grotius and Selden.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

Library collections
-------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Library collections")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Bodleian_Library_Arch._B_f.69.png/250px-Bodleian_Library_Arch._B_f.69.png)](/wiki/File:Bodleian_Library_Arch._B_f.69.png)

Title page for John Selden's copy of *Sanctos no gosagues no uchi nuqigaqi quan dai ichi* (1591). This was the first book printed with moveable type in Japan. Oxford, Bodleian Library Arch. B f.69: https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/3bdc1c46-9c84-4e64-aa83-b48b4baf2a5f//

By the time of his death in 1654, Selden had accumulated a library of several thousand manuscripts and printed books. Selden's will left his intentions for this library somewhat ambiguous, although the will and [codicil](/wiki/Codicil_(will) "Codicil (will)") seem to suggest that he intended to bequeath most of his [Oriental](/wiki/Orient "Orient") manuscripts, Greek manuscripts, a Latin manuscript, and his printed [Talmudic](/wiki/Talmud "Talmud") and [Rabbinical](/wiki/Rabbinic_literature "Rabbinic literature") books to the [Bodleian Library](/wiki/Bodleian_Library "Bodleian Library"), Oxford.[[45]](#cite_note-45) There is some evidence to suggest that Selden intended to leave his printed books and historical manuscripts to the [Inner Temple](/wiki/Inner_Temple "Inner Temple") but that this transaction did not occur because the Temple did not possess a large enough library.[[46]](#cite_note-46) By 1656, two years after Selden's death, his executors (Edward Heyward, John Vaughan, [Matthew Hale](/wiki/Matthew_Hale_(jurist) "Matthew Hale (jurist)"), and Rowland Jewks) were in negotiation with the Bodleian library to transfer Selden's entire collection.[[47]](#cite_note-:0-47) In 1659, the executors stipulated that Selden's manuscripts "bee forever heerafter kepte together in one distincte pile and body under the name of Mr. Selden’s Library." The Bodleian agreed, and the library received Selden's collection in June 1659.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._c.2_cover.png/250px-Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._c.2_cover.png)](/wiki/File:Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._c.2_cover.png)

Cover of John Selden's copy of Boccaccio's *Decamerone*. The design on the cover is similar to the Plantagenet crest. Holes from clasps are also visible. Oxford, Bodleian Library S. Seld. c.2: https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/61459688-0512-49e0-a996-a4f0921956b2/

Selden's collection was the largest received by the Bodleian in the seventeenth century, comprising around 8,000 items.[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) Even this massive collection did not represent the extent of Selden's library. Duplicates, meaning books the library already owned, were given to [Gloucester Cathedral](/wiki/Gloucester_Cathedral "Gloucester Cathedral") library.[[47]](#cite_note-:0-47) A rumour also circulated in the decades after Selden's death that part of his library had remained in London and was destroyed by a fire. The 1704 edition of [Edward Chamberlayne](/wiki/Edward_Chamberlayne "Edward Chamberlayne")'s *The Present State of England* claimed that a fire at the Inner Temple destroyed "8 Chests full" of Selden's manuscripts.[[50]](#cite_note-50) Still, the collection the Bodleian received was large enough that it required several years and multiple librarians to fully catalogue.[[51]](#cite_note-51) Since then, the original collection has been enhanced by further acquisitions, most notably by a group of forty Selden manuscripts purchased by the Bodleian from James Fairhurst in 1947.[[52]](#cite_note-52)[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) The Selden collection at the Bodleian houses more than 400 manuscript volumes taking up more than 40 meters (approx. 130 feet) of shelf space.[[53]](#cite_note-53)[[54]](#cite_note-54) The linguistic range of these manuscripts reflects Selden's interest in eastern and other languages. The languages represented include

* Russian
  + An incomplete Russian-English vocabulary (MS. Selden Supra 61)
  + Samples of Russian [calligraphy](/wiki/Calligraphy "Calligraphy") (MS. Arch. Selden A. 72 (5))
* Greek
  + Astronomical and musical treatises (MS. Arch. Selden B. 17)
  + Several Greek versions of the [New Testament](/wiki/New_Testament "New Testament") [Gospels](/wiki/Gospel "Gospel") (MS. Selden Supra 2, 3, 6, 28–9)
* Arabic
  + Prayers, meditations, and [Quranic](/wiki/Quran "Quran") praises (MS. Selden Superius 3)
  + Works on [astrology](/wiki/Astrology "Astrology") and medicine (MS. Selden Superius 15)
  + Works on [Algebra](/wiki/Algebra "Algebra") and mathematics (MS. Selden Superius 65)
* Hebrew
  + [Hebrew](/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language") and [Arabic](/wiki/Arabic "Arabic") grammar and vocabulary (MS. Selden Supra 107)
  + [Kabbalah](/wiki/Kabbalah "Kabbalah") and Kabbalistic collections (MS. Arch. Selden A. 56; MS. Selden Superius 107)
* New World languages
  + A treatise on Mexican hieroglyphics (MS. Arch. Selden A. 2)

Many manuscripts relate to Selden's study of the law both in England and internationally. These include

* A fragment on Islamic law (MS. Selden Superius 42)
* [Canon law](/wiki/Canon_law "Canon law") (MS. Arch. Selden A. 63)
* An account of the laws of [Ivan the Terrible](/wiki/Ivan_the_Terrible "Ivan the Terrible") (MS. Selden Supra. 59)
* Various legal topics, such as maritime law and a Latin treatise on procedure in Civil Courts (MS. Arch. Selden B. 27)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._e.2.png/250px-Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._e.2.png)](/wiki/File:Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._e.2.png)

A heavily annotated page in John Selden's copy of Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, translated by Leonardus Brunus Aretinus (1479). The page includes a space left for an [initial](/wiki/Initial "Initial") (also called a drop cap). Oxford, Bodleian Library S. Seld. e.2: https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/032cc92a-b24c-48ab-9c58-3545cf24121f/.

Some manuscripts touch on contemporary events. For instance MS. Arch. Selden B. 8 includes a Latin speech given in Oxford on the return of [Prince Charles from Spain in 1623](/wiki/Spanish_match "Spanish match"). Still others contain classical works of philosophy and literature, such as

* Treatises of Aristotle (MS. Selden Supra 24)
* [Aeschylus](/wiki/Aeschylus "Aeschylus") and [Lycophron](/wiki/Lycophron "Lycophron") (MS. Selden Supra 18)

Beyond manuscripts, the Selden collection contains several notable printed works. Among them is the first book ever printed in Japan using moveable type, *Sanctos no gosagueo no uchi nuqigaqi* (Arch.b.f.69).[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) The printed books included in the Selden collection contain many that are significant in part because they originated in the libraries of other famous figures, including [Sir Robert Cotton](/wiki/Sir_Robert_Cotton,_1st_Baronet,_of_Connington "Sir Robert Cotton, 1st Baronet, of Connington"), [John Donne](/wiki/John_Donne "John Donne"), and [John Dee](/wiki/John_Dee "John Dee").[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) According to [Geoffrey Keynes](/wiki/Geoffrey_Keynes "Geoffrey Keynes"), several of the books Selden received from John Donne's library include inscriptions from both men. One such book is [Theodorus Beza](/wiki/Theodore_Beza "Theodore Beza")'s *Tractatio de polygamia*, which includes Donne's signature and motto ("Per Rachel ho servitor, & non per Lea"), as well as Selden's motto ("περί παντός τήν έλευθερίαν", "Freedom above all things").[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-56)

It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Background\")]\\n\\nThe *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics \"Apologetics\")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts \"Milton\\'s antiprelatical tracts\"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\").[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Tract\")]\\n\\nMilton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) \"as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded\".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) \"that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call\\'d regenerate reason\".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:\\n\\n> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Themes\")]\\n\\nThe *Apology*, like many of Milton\\'s other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual\\'s character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how \"Milton\\'s self is produced in the process of writing\" and that his self is put through \"a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations\".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains \"Milton\\'s understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle \"Aristotle\")\\'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange.\"[[9]](#cite_note-9)\\n\\nSee also\\n--------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: See also\")]\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Notes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Wheeler 2003 p. 273\\n2. **[^](#cite_ref-2)** Wheeler 2003 pp. 273–274\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** Milton 1953 p. 871\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-Wheeler_p._275_4-1) Wheeler 2003 p. 274\\n5. **[^](#cite_ref-5)** Milton 1953 p. 874\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** Milton 1953 p. 890\\n7. **[^](#cite_ref-7)** Keeble 2003 p. 132\\n8. **[^](#cite_ref-8)** Stevens 1988 p. 268\\n9. **[^](#cite_ref-9)** Wheeler 2003 p. 275\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n* Keeble, N. [g]\")\\n\\nAppearance\\n\\nmove to sidebar\\nhide\\n\\nFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\\n\\nGroup of clergy active in 1641 England\\n\\n**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name \"Pen name\")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan \"Puritan\") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England \"England\") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland \"Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland\"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) \"Thomas Young (1587-1655)\")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.\\n\\nThe name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) \"Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)\"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder \"Edmund Calamy the Elder\"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen \"Matthew Newcomen\"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow \"William Spurstow\"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall\\'s](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) \"Joseph Hall (bishop)\") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton \"John Milton\") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus\\'s reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)\\n\\nThis response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.\\n\\nMilton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions \"Animadversions\")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus \"Apology for Smectymnuus\")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-1)** Hoover, David L.; Corns, Thomas N. Please help to [improve](/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Reliability \"Wikipedia:WikiProject Reliability\") this article by [introducing](/wiki/Wikipedia:When_to_cite \"Wikipedia:When to cite\") more precise citations. *(February 2012)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal \"Help:Maintenance template removal\"))* |  *([Learn how and when to remove this message](/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal \"Help:Maintenance template removal\"))* |\\n\\n**Stephen Marshall** (c.\\u20091594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England \"England\") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) \"Nonconformist (Protestantism)\") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym \"John Pym\") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only \"systematic\" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism \"Infant Baptism\")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes \"John Tombes\") (1646).\\n\\nEarly life\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Early life\")]\\n\\nHe was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester \"Godmanchester\") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire \"Huntingdonshire\"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge \"Emmanuel College, Cambridge\") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex \"Wethersfield, Essex\") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England \"Essex, England\"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield \"Finchingfield\"). In 1636 he was reported for \"want of conformity.\"\\n\\nCivil War years\\n---------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Civil War years\")]\\n\\nMarshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie \"Robert Baillie\") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament \"Short Parliament\") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon \"Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon\") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud \"William Laud\") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret\\'s, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster \"St. Margaret\\'s, Westminster\"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.\\n\\nHe had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex\\'s regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment \"Earl of Essex\\'s regiment\") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland \"Scotland\") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference \"Uxbridge Conference\") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter\\'s execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House \"Holmby House\") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle \"Carisbrooke Castle\").\\n\\nLater life\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Later life\")]\\n\\nA moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian \"Presbyterian\"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism \"Westminster Shorter Catechism\") in 1647, and was one of the \"Triers\" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey \"Westminster Abbey\"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration \"English Restoration\").\\n\\nWorks\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: Works\")]\\n\\n* [A defence of infant-baptism in answer to two treatises](//archive.org/details/defenceofinfantb00mars \"iarchive:defenceofinfantb00mars\")\\n\\nHe worked as a contributor on:\\n\\n* [Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus \"Smectymnuus\") (contributor)\\n* [Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Shorter_Catechism \"Shorter Catechism\") (contributor)\\n\\n### Sermons\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Sermons\")]\\n\\n* [A sermon Preached before the Honourable House of Commons, now assembled in Parliament](//archive.org/details/asermonpreached00marsgoog \"iarchive:asermonpreached00marsgoog\"), at their publike Fast, 17 November 1640. For the English rugby union player, see [John Pym (rugby union, born 1891)](/wiki/John_Pym_(rugby_union,_born_1891) \"John Pym (rugby union, born 1891)\").\\n\\n| John Pym  [MP](/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) \"Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)\") [JP](/wiki/Justice_of_the_Peace#United_Kingdom \"Justice of the Peace\") | |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Pym, c. 1640 | |\\n|  | |\\n| [Committee of Safety](/wiki/Committee_of_Safety_(England) \"Committee of Safety (England)\") | |\\n| **In office** July 1642\\xa0– December 1643 | |\\n| Monarch | [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\") |\\n| [Member of Parliament](/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) \"Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)\") | |\\n| **In office** 1624\\xa0– 8 December 1643 | |\\n| Preceded by | [Baptist Hicks](/wiki/Baptist_Hicks,_1st_Viscount_Campden \"Baptist Hicks, 1st Viscount Campden\") |\\n| Succeeded by | [Edmund Fowell](/wiki/Edmund_Fowell \"Edmund Fowell\") |\\n| Constituency | [Tavistock](/wiki/Tavistock_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Tavistock (UK Parliament constituency)\") |\\n| **In office** 1621–1622 | |\\n| Preceded by | Richard Lowe |\\n| Succeeded by | [Edward Howard](/wiki/Edward_Howard,_1st_Baron_Howard_of_Escrick \"Edward Howard, 1st Baron Howard of Escrick\") |\\n| Constituency | [Calne](/wiki/Calne_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Calne (UK Parliament constituency)\") |\\n| Receiver-General [Exchequer](/wiki/Exchequer \"Exchequer\"), Glos., Hants and Wilts. | |\\n| **In office** 1606–1639 | |\\n|  | |\\n| Personal details | |\\n| Born | (1584-05-20)20 May 1584  [London](/wiki/London \"London\"), England |\\n| Died | 8 December 1643(1643-12-08) (aged\\xa059)  London, England |\\n| Cause\\xa0of\\xa0death | Cancer |\\n| Resting place | [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey \"Westminster Abbey\") (initially);  [St Margaret\\'s](/wiki/St_Margaret%27s,_Westminster \"St Margaret\\'s, Westminster\") (now) |\\n| Spouse | Anne Hooker or Hooke (1604–1620) |\\n| Children | 7, including [Charles](/wiki/Sir_Charles_Pym,_1st_Baronet \"Sir Charles Pym, 1st Baronet\") |\\n| Parent(s) | Alexander Pym (1547–1585)   Philippa Colles |\\n| Relatives | [Francis Rous](/wiki/Francis_Rous \"Francis Rous\") (stepbrother)  [Anthony Nicholl](/wiki/Anthony_Nicholl \"Anthony Nicholl\") (nephew) |\\n| [Alma mater](/wiki/Alma_mater \"Alma mater\") | [Pembroke College, Oxford](/wiki/Pembroke_College,_Oxford \"Pembroke College, Oxford\") |\\n| Occupation | Lawyer, politician and businessman |\\n| Movement | [Parliamentarians](/wiki/Roundhead \"Roundhead\") |\\n|  | |\\n\\n**John Pym** (20 May 1584 – 8 December 1643) was a politician from [Somerset](/wiki/Somerset \"Somerset\") who played a key role in establishing the modern [English Parliamentary system](/wiki/Westminster_system \"Westminster system\"). One of the [Five Members](/wiki/Five_Members \"Five Members\") whose attempted arrest in January 1642 was a major step in sparking the [First English Civil War](/wiki/First_English_Civil_War \"First English Civil War\"), his use of procedure to outmanoeuvre opponents was unusual for the period. Though this meant he was respected by contemporaries rather than admired, in 1895 historian [Goldwin Smith](/wiki/Goldwin_Smith \"Goldwin Smith\") described him as \"the greatest member of Parliament that ever lived\".[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196938-1)\\n\\nPym\\'s father died when he was seven months old, and he was raised by his stepfather Sir [Anthony Rous](/wiki/Anthony_Rous_(1555-1620) \"Anthony Rous (1555-1620)\"), from whom he inherited his [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan \"Puritan\") views and deep opposition to [Archbishop Laud](/wiki/Archbishop_Laud \"Archbishop Laud\")\\'s [reforms](/wiki/Arminianism_in_the_Church_of_England \"Arminianism in the Church of England\"). He was also a leading member of the [Providence Island Company](/wiki/Providence_Island_Company \"Providence Island Company\"), which attempted to establish a Puritan colony in Central America.\\n\\nDescribed as \\'a true revolutionary\\', he led the opposition to arbitrary rule first under [James I](/wiki/James_I_of_England \"James I of England\"), then [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\"). His leadership in the early stages of the war was essential to the Parliamentarian cause, particularly his role in negotiating the [Solemn League and Covenant](/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant \"Solemn League and Covenant\") with the Scots [Covenanters](/wiki/Covenanters \"Covenanters\"); his death from cancer in December 1643 was considered a major blow.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2004278-2)\\n\\nOriginally buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey \"Westminster Abbey\"),[[3]](#cite_note-3) after the [Stuart Restoration](/wiki/Stuart_Restoration \"Stuart Restoration\") in 1660, his body was dumped in a pit at nearby [St Margaret\\'s, Westminster](/wiki/St_Margaret%27s,_Westminster \"St Margaret\\'s, Westminster\") along with those of other Parliamentary leaders.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStanley1882204–205-4) Though his reputation later suffered in comparison to less complex figures like [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden \"John Hampden\") and [Viscount Falkland](/wiki/Lucius_Cary,_2nd_Viscount_Falkland \"Lucius Cary, 2nd Viscount Falkland\"), he is now viewed as an astute politician and effective speaker. Many of his ideas were adopted by [Patriots during the American Revolution](/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution) \"Patriot (American Revolution)\") and 19th-century [American liberals](/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States \"Liberalism in the United States\").[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKuypersAlthouse2009225–245-5)\\n\\nPersonal details\\n----------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Pym&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Personal details\")]\\n\\nHis father, [Alexander Pym](/wiki/Alexander_Pym \"Alexander Pym\") (1547–1585), was a member of the minor gentry from Brymore in [Somerset](/wiki/Somerset \"Somerset\"), and a successful lawyer in [London](/wiki/London \"London\"), where John was born in 1584. Alexander died seven months later and his mother, Philippa Colles (died 1620), married a wealthy Cornish landowner, Sir [Anthony Rous](/wiki/Anthony_Rous_(died_1620) \"Anthony Rous (died 1620)\").[[6]](#cite_note-6) A close friend and [executor](/wiki/Executor \"Executor\") of Sir [Francis Drake](/wiki/Francis_Drake \"Francis Drake\"), Sir Anthony instilled in his stepson[[7]](#cite_note-HistParl-7) a strong dislike of [Spain](/wiki/Habsburg_Spain \"Habsburg Spain\"), a zealous [Puritanism](/wiki/Puritanism \"Puritanism\"), and opposition to both the [Catholic Church](/wiki/Catholic_Church \"Catholic Church\"), and the rival Protestant theology of [Arminianism](/wiki/Arminianism \"Arminianism\").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussell1990221-8)\\n\\nThe Rous were a large and close-knit family, often wedding relatives and friends. In May 1604, Pym married Anne Hooke, a daughter of Barbara Rous and John Hooke, and aunt of the scientist [Robert Hooke](/wiki/Robert_Hooke \"Robert Hooke\"). Before her death in 1620, they had seven children, of whom four survived into adulthood; Philippa (1604–1654), [Charles](/wiki/Sir_Charles_Pym,_1st_Baronet \"Sir Charles Pym, 1st Baronet\") (1615–1671), Dorothy (1617–1661), and Catherine.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196943-9)\\n\\nCareer\\n------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Pym&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Career\")]\\n\\nPym was educated at [Pembroke College, Oxford](/wiki/Pembroke_College,_Oxford \"Pembroke College, Oxford\"), then known as Broadgates and famous for \\'advanced Protestantism\\'.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcGee2004406-10) Since legal knowledge was considered part of an education, he subsequently attended the [Middle Temple](/wiki/Middle_Temple \"Middle Temple\") in 1602; while he does not appear to have formally graduated from either, he made a number of lifelong friends, the most important of which being [William Whitaker](/wiki/William_Whitaker_(MP) \"William Whitaker (MP)\").[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196942-11)\\n\\nIn June 1605, he was appointed collector of taxes for the [Exchequer](/wiki/Exchequer \"Exchequer\") in [Hampshire](/wiki/Hampshire \"Hampshire\"), [Gloucestershire](/wiki/Gloucestershire \"Gloucestershire\"), and [Wiltshire](/wiki/Wiltshire \"Wiltshire\"); this gave him a broader range of connections than many contemporaries, who were often confined to family or county networks. Whitaker\\'s father had been [Member of Parliament](/wiki/Member_of_Parliament \"Member of Parliament\") for [Westbury, Wiltshire](/wiki/Westbury_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Westbury (UK Parliament constituency)\"), and in 1621, Pym was elected for the nearby seat of [Calne](/wiki/Calne_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Calne (UK Parliament constituency)\").[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrisHunneyball2010-12)\\n\\n### Forced Loan and Petition of Right\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Pym&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: Forced Loan and Petition of Right\")]\\n\\nPym\\'s diary shows he viewed Parliamentary legislation as a whole, not just issues of interest to himself; combined with an ability to explain them clearly, it led to his appointment to numerous committees. Since direct criticism of the king was considered treason, the only way to express opposition was by attacking his advisors, using the process of [impeachment](/wiki/Impeachment_in_the_United_Kingdom \"Impeachment in the United Kingdom\"). Pym argued it was for the [Commons](/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England \"House of Commons of England\") to decide guilt or innocence, leaving the [Lords](/wiki/House_of_Lords \"House of Lords\") only to determine the penalty; this would become significant in his future Parliamentary career.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrisHunneyball2010-12)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Francis%2C_4th_Earl_of_Bedford_by_Henry_Bone.jpg/250px-Francis%2C_4th_Earl_of_Bedford_by_Henry_Bone.jpg)](/wiki/File:Francis,_4th_Earl_of_Bedford_by_Henry_Bone.jpg)\\n\\nPym\\'s patron and political ally, the [Earl of Bedford](/wiki/Francis_Russell,_4th_Earl_of_Bedford \"Francis Russell, 4th Earl of Bedford\"), 1587–1641\\n\\nEven in an era when it was common, he was notable for his anti-Catholicism, and opposition to alleged [Catholic practices in the Church of England](/wiki/Arminianism_in_the_Church_of_England \"Arminianism in the Church of England\"). One reason for this was the close links in the 17th-century between religion and politics, with alterations in one viewed as implying alterations in the other. Many contemporaries fought in the [Thirty Years\\' War](/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War \"Thirty Years\\' War\") and were concerned at the apparent failure of [James](/wiki/James_I_of_England \"James I of England\") to defend [Frederick](/wiki/Frederick_V_of_the_Palatinate \"Frederick V of the Palatinate\") the [elector of Palatine](/wiki/Elector_of_Palatine \"Elector of Palatine\"), his own son-in-law, and so [Protestant Europe](/wiki/Protestantism \"Protestantism\") as a whole.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196945–50-13)\\n\\nFollowing the dissolution of Parliament in 1621, Pym was arrested, and brought before the [Privy Council](/wiki/Privy_Council_of_England \"Privy Council of England\"), but released in August 1622. In 1624, he was elected for [Tavistock](/wiki/Tavistock_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Tavistock (UK Parliament constituency)\"), a seat controlled by [Earl of Bedford](/wiki/Francis_Russell,_4th_Earl_of_Bedford \"Francis Russell, 4th Earl of Bedford\"), which he retained for the rest of his career.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrisHunneyball2010-12) In 1626, he led an attempt to impeach the [Duke of Buckingham](/wiki/George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of_Buckingham \"George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham\"), an action which led to Parliament being dissolved. Only Buckingham\\'s assassination in August 1628 prevented a second attempt, while Pym supported the presentation of the [Petition of Right](/wiki/Petition_of_Right \"Petition of Right\") to [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\") in 1628.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrisHunneyball2010-12)\\n\\nPym, his stepbrother [Francis Rous](/wiki/Francis_Rous \"Francis Rous\"), and [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden \"John Hampden\"), also led the Parliamentary attack on [Roger Maynwaring](/wiki/Roger_Maynwaring \"Roger Maynwaring\") and [Robert Sibthorpe](/wiki/Robert_Sibthorpe \"Robert Sibthorpe\"), two clergymen who published [sermons](/wiki/Sermons \"Sermons\") supporting the Caroline precepts of the [divine right of kings](/wiki/Divine_right_of_kings \"Divine right of kings\"), and [passive obedience](/wiki/Passive_obedience \"Passive obedience\"). Though [censured](/wiki/Censured \"Censured\") by Parliament for preaching against the established English constitution, Charles [pardoned](/wiki/Royal_prerogative_of_mercy \"Royal prerogative of mercy\") them, and [dissolved Parliament](/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Parliament_of_England \"Dissolution of the Parliament of England\"), initiating the period of [Personal Rule](/wiki/Personal_Rule \"Personal Rule\") that continued until 1640.[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELittle200833-14)\\n\\nPym became treasurer of the [Providence Island Company](/wiki/Providence_Island_Company \"Providence Island Company\") in 1630, a role that increasingly consumed his time, and he relinquished his Exchequer position in 1639. Participation in the colonial movement was common among Puritan leaders, while company meetings later provided cover for co-ordinating political opposition. Many of these became leaders of the Parliamentary opposition in 1642, among them Hampden, Rous, Henry Darley, [Lord Saye](/wiki/William_Fiennes,_1st_Viscount_Saye_and_Sele \"William Fiennes, 1st Viscount Saye and Sele\"), [William Waller](/wiki/William_Waller \"William Waller\"), and [Lord Brooke](/wiki/Robert_Greville,_2nd_Baron_Brooke \"Robert Greville, 2nd Baron Brooke\").[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVan_Duinen2007531-15)\\n\\n### Leader of the opposition; 1640 to 1641\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Pym&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: Leader of the opposition; 1640 to 1641\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/John_Hampden_portrait.jpg/250px-John_Hampden_portrait.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Hampden_portrait.jpg)\\n\\n[John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden \"John Hampden\"); Pym\\'s colleague, and one of the [Five Members](/wiki/Five_Members \"Five Members\")\\n\\nFollowing defeat in the first of the [Bishops Wars](/wiki/Bishops_Wars \"Bishops Wars\"), Charles recalled Parliament in April 1640. When the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament \"Short Parliament\") refused to vote him taxes without political concessions, he dissolved it after only three weeks. When the [Treaty of Ripon](/wiki/Treaty_of_Ripon \"Treaty of Ripon\") imposed by the Scots after a second defeat forced him to hold fresh elections in November, Pym became the unofficial leader of the opposition.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJessup201325-16)\\n\\nHistorians like [Tim Harris](/wiki/Timothy_J._G._Harris \"Timothy J. G. Harris\") argue that, with the exception of a few extremists, by 1640 there was general consensus attempts to rule without Parliament had gone too far. This changed after the [Grand Remonstrance](/wiki/Grand_Remonstrance \"Grand Remonstrance\") in November 1641, when [constitutional monarchists](/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy \"Constitutional monarchy\") like Clarendon switched sides, arguing Parliament now wanted too much.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2014457–458-17)\\n\\nWhere Pym differed from Clarendon, and many of his own colleagues, was recognising Charles would not keep commitments he felt had been forced from him. Even during negotiations with Parliament, he and [Henrietta Maria](/wiki/Henrietta_Maria_of_France \"Henrietta Maria of France\") openly told foreign ambassadors any concessions were temporary, and would be retrieved by force if needed. These suspicions increased after [October 1641](/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 \"Irish Rebellion of 1641\"), when Irish Catholic rebels claimed his approval for their actions. Many believed them, given previous attempts by Charles to use Irish troops against the Scots, and his initial refusal to condemn the rebellion.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood200126–27-18)\\n\\nHowever, Pym was hampered by the fact Charles was essential to a stable government and society. Regardless of religion or political belief, in 1642 the vast majority believed a \\'well-ordered\\' monarchy was divinely mandated; where they disagreed was what \\'well-ordered\\' meant, and who held ultimate authority in clerical affairs. [Royalists](/wiki/Cavalier \"Cavalier\") generally supported a [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\") governed by [bishops](/wiki/Episcopal_polity \"Episcopal polity\"), appointed by, and answerable to, the king; [Parliamentarians](/wiki/Roundhead \"Roundhead\") were often more more friendly to [Puritanism](/wiki/Puritanism \"Puritanism\") which tended to hold that church leaders should be appointed either by [their congregations](/wiki/Congregationalism \"Congregationalism\") or [assemblies of elders](/wiki/English_Presbyterianism \"English Presbyterianism\").[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECraig200839-19)\\n\\n[Puritan](/wiki/Puritan \"Puritan\") was a term for anyone who wanted to reform, or \\'purify\\', the Church of England, and contained many different sects. [Presbyterians](/wiki/Presbyterian_polity \"Presbyterian polity\") were the most prominent, and included leaders like Pym and [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden \"John Hampden\"), but there were many others, such as [Congregationalists](/wiki/Congregational_church \"Congregational church\"), often grouped together as [Independents](/wiki/Independent_(religion) \"Independent (religion)\"). Close links between religion and politics added further complexity; one reason for opposition to bishops was their presence in the [House of Lords](/wiki/House_of_Lords \"House of Lords\"), where they often blocked Parliamentary legislation. Their removal by the [Clergy Act 1640](/wiki/Clergy_Act_1640 \"Clergy Act 1640\") was a major step along the road to war.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood200131-20)\\n\\nMost Presbyterians were political conservatives, who believed in a limited electorate, and wanted to keep the Church of England, but as a reformed, Presbyterian body, similar to the [Church of Scotland](/wiki/Church_of_Scotland \"Church of Scotland\"). In general, England was a structured, socially conservative, and largely peaceful society, while the devastation caused by the Thirty Years\\' War meant many wanted to avoid conflict at any cost. Pym was one of the few who believed only military defeat would force Charles into agreeing meaningful reforms.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood2001253-21)\\n\\n### Road to war; 1641 to 1643\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Pym&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Road to war; 1641 to 1643\")]\\n\\nShortly after the [Long Parliament](/wiki/Long_Parliament \"Long Parliament\") assembled, it was presented with the [Root and Branch petition](/wiki/Root_and_Branch_petition \"Root and Branch petition\"); signed by 15,000 Londoners, it demanded England follow the Scots, and expel bishops.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERees20162-22) This reflected widespread concerns about \\'Catholic practices\\', or [Arminianism in the Church of England](/wiki/Arminianism_in_the_Church_of_England \"Arminianism in the Church of England\"), given weight by Charles\\' apparent willingness to make war on the Protestant Scots, but not assist his nephew [Charles Louis](/wiki/Charles_I_Louis,_Elector_Palatine \"Charles I Louis, Elector Palatine\") regain his [hereditary lands](/wiki/Electoral_Palatinate \"Electoral Palatinate\").[[a]](#cite_note-23) Many feared Charles was about to sign an alliance with Spain, a view shared by experienced diplomatic observers like [Venice](/wiki/Republic_of_Venice \"Republic of Venice\"), and even France.[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWedgwood1983248-24)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Wenceslas_Hollar_-_Trial_of_Strafford_%28State_2%29_cropped.jpg/250px-Wenceslas_Hollar_-_Trial_of_Strafford_%28State_2%29_cropped.jpg)](/wiki/File:Wenceslas_Hollar_-_Trial_of_Strafford_(State_2)_cropped.jpg)\\n\\nThe trial of [the Earl of Strafford](/wiki/Thomas_Wentworth,_1st_Earl_of_Strafford \"Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford\"), March 1641\\n\\nThis meant ending Charles\\' arbitrary rule was not only important for England, but the Protestant cause in general. Since respect for the institution of monarchy prevented direct attacks on Charles, the traditional route was to prosecute his \\'evil counsellors.\\' Doing so made it clear that although the king was above the law, his subordinates were not, and he could not protect them; the intention was to make others think twice about their actions. Archbishop [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud \"William Laud\") was impeached in December 1640 and held in the [Tower of London](/wiki/Tower_of_London \"Tower of London\") until his execution in 1645; [Strafford](/wiki/Thomas_Wentworth,_1st_Earl_of_Strafford \"Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford\"), former [Lord Deputy of Ireland](/wiki/Lord_Deputy_of_Ireland \"Lord Deputy of Ireland\") and organiser of the 1640 Bishops War, was [attainted](/wiki/Attainder \"Attainder\") and executed in May 1641.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerrisHunneyball2010-12) Although it\\'s disputed, Pym\\'s appearance at the trial may have been the origin of the word [Roundhead](/wiki/Roundhead \"Roundhead\"). According to [Richard Baxter](/wiki/Richard_Baxter \"Richard Baxter\") Queen [Henrietta Maria](/wiki/Henrietta_Maria_of_France \"Henrietta Maria of France\") at the trial of [Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford](/wiki/Thomas_Wentworth,_1st_Earl_of_Strafford \"Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford\") in 1641 asking about Pym asked who the roundheaded man was.[[24]](#cite_note-25)\\n\\nThe Commons also passed a series of constitutional reforms, including the [Triennial Act 1640](/wiki/Triennial_Act_1640 \"Triennial Act 1640\") ([16 Cha. 1](/wiki/16_Cha._1 \"16 Cha. 1\"). c. 1), abolition of the [Star Chamber](/wiki/Star_Chamber \"Star Chamber\"), and an end to levying taxes without Parliament\\'s consent. Voting as a block, the bishops ensured all these were rejected by the Lords.[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERees20167–8-26) In June 1641, Pym secured passage of the Clergy Act in the Commons; one of its key provisions was to remove bishops from the Lords, which therefore rejected it. The growing political tension was brought to head in October with the outbreak of the [Irish Rebellion](/wiki/Irish_Rebellion_of_1641 \"Irish Rebellion of 1641\"). both Charles and Parliament supported raising troops to suppress it, but neither trusted the other with their control, fearing any army would be used against them first.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHutton20034-27)\\n\\nPym helped draft the [Grand Remonstrance](/wiki/Grand_Remonstrance \"Grand Remonstrance\"), presented to Charles on 1 December 1641; unrest culminated in 23 to 29 December with widespread riots in [Westminster](/wiki/Westminster \"Westminster\"), led by the London apprentices. Suggestions Pym and other Parliamentary leaders helped organise these have not been proved, but as a result, bishops stopped attending the Lords.[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1979315–317-28) On 30 December, [John Williams](/wiki/John_Williams_(archbishop_of_York) \"John Williams (archbishop of York)\"), [Archbishop of York](/wiki/Archbishop_of_York \"Archbishop of York\") and eleven other bishops, signed a complaint, disputing the legality of any laws passed by the Lords during their exclusion. Viewed by the Commons as inviting Charles to dissolve Parliament, all twelve were imprisoned for treason.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERees20169–10-29)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Attempted_Arrest_of_the_Five_members_by_Charles_West_Cope.jpg/250px-Attempted_Arrest_of_the_Five_members_by_Charles_West_Cope.jpg)](/wiki/File:Attempted_Arrest_of_the_Five_members_by_Charles_West_Cope.jpg)\\n\\nVictorian re-imagining of the arrest the [Five Members](/wiki/Five_Members \"Five Members\"), January 1642\\n\\nIn response to the growing unrest, on 4 January Charles made an unsuccessful attempt to arrest the [Five Members](/wiki/Five_Members \"Five Members\"), one of whom was Pym. Having failed to do so, he left London accompanied by many [Royalist](/wiki/Cavaliers \"Cavaliers\") MPs and his supporters in the Lords, a major tactical mistake as it gave the opposition majorities in both houses.[[29]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEManganiello200460-30) When the [First English Civil War](/wiki/First_English_Civil_War \"First English Civil War\") began in August, Pym headed the [Committee of Safety](/wiki/English_Committee_of_Safety \"English Committee of Safety\"); his reputation for integrity and ability to keep a diverse coalition of interests together was crucial to surviving the first 18 months of the conflict.[[30]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196937-31)\\n\\nBy early August 1643, a series of Royalist victories combined with the death in June of the popular [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden \"John Hampden\") in the [Battle of Chalgrove Field](/wiki/Battle_of_Chalgrove_Field \"Battle of Chalgrove Field\") meant the Parliamentarian cause seemed close to collapse. At this crucial point, it was saved by Pym\\'s leadership and determination, which led to a renewed commitment to win the war.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJohnson2012172–174-32) He created the foundations of victory by ensuring Parliament had sufficient financial and military resources, one of his last acts being to negotiate the [Solemn League and Covenant](/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant \"Solemn League and Covenant\") that secured Scottish support.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussell2009-33) Amidst the escalating tensions, one particular step Pym took played a major role in consolidating Parliament\\'s authority. He orchestrated the expulsion of [Henry Marten](/wiki/Henry_Marten_(regicide) \"Henry Marten (regicide)\"), a fellow Parliamentarian known for his radical views and outspoken criticism of the monarchy. Marten had publicly advocated for the deposition of King Charles I, a stance deemed too extreme by many in Parliament. Pym seized upon this opportunity to remove Marten, demonstrating his commitment to maintaining a more moderate and unified Parliamentarian front. Historian [David Como](/wiki/David_Como \"David Como\") believes this manoeuvre underscores Pym\\'s political acumen and his influence within Parliament during this critical period.[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEComo2018177-34)\\n\\nHe died, probably of cancer, at Derby House on 8 December 1643; Parliament agreed to pay off the debts he incurred as a result of neglecting his private business interests, although they were still being disputed in 1665.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoyle2004278-2) Buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey \"Westminster Abbey\"), his remains were exhumed after the [Stuart Restoration](/wiki/Stuart_Restoration \"Stuart Restoration\") in 1660 and re-buried in a common pit at [St Margaret\\'s, Westminster](/wiki/St_Margaret%27s,_Westminster \"St Margaret\\'s, Westminster\").[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStanley1882204–205-4)\\n\\nHis chief opponent, the [Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon \"Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon\"), a senior advisor to Charles during the [First English Civil War](/wiki/First_English_Civil_War \"First English Civil War\"), later wrote; \\'he had a very comely and grave way of expressing himself...and understood the temper and affections of the kingdom as well as any man\\'.[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEClarendon2019321–322-35) Pym\\'s reputation suffered in comparison to less complex figures like Hampden and [Viscount Falkland](/wiki/Lucius_Cary,_2nd_Viscount_Falkland \"Lucius Cary, 2nd Viscount Falkland\"), especially during the [Victorian era](/wiki/Victorian_era \"Victorian era\") which romanticised the Royalist cause. One exception was the historian [Goldwin Smith](/wiki/Goldwin_Smith \"Goldwin Smith\"), who described him as \"the greatest member of Parliament that ever lived\".[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196938-1) He is now generally viewed as an astute politician who laid the foundations of modern Parliamentary democracy and effective speaker, whose ideas and language were adapted by [Patriots during the American Revolution](/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution) \"Patriot (American Revolution)\") and [19th century American liberals](/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States \"Liberalism in the United States\").[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKuypersAlthouse2009225–245-5)\\n\\nFootnotes\\n---------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Pym&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: Footnotes\")]\\n\\n1. **[^](#cite_ref-23)** A perspective summarised by Pym\\'s stepbrother Francis in 1641; \"For Arminianism is the span of a Papist, and if you mark it well, you shall see an Arminian reaching to a Papist, a Papist to a Jesuit, a Jesuit to the Pope, and the other to the King of Spain. And having kindled fire in our neighbours, they now seek to set on flame this kingdom also.\"\\n\\nReferences\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Pym&action=edit&section=7 \"Edit section: References\")]\\n\\n1. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196938_1-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacDonald196938_1-1) [MacDonald 1969](#CITEREFMacDonald1969), p.\\xa038.\\n2. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoyle2004278_2-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTERoyle2004278_2-1) [Royle 2004](#CITEREFRoyle2004), p.\\xa0278.\\n3. **[^](#cite_ref-3)** [Stanley, A.P.](/wiki/Arthur_Penrhyn_Stanley \"Arthur Penrhyn Stanley\"), *Historical Memorials of Westminster Abbey* ([London](/wiki/London \"London\"); [John Murray](/wiki/John_Murray_(publishing_house) \"John Murray (publishing house)\"); 1882), p. 204.\\n4. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEStanley1882204–205_4-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEStanley1882204–205_4-1) [Stanley 1882](#CITEREFStanley1882), pp.\\xa0204–205.\\n5. ^ [***a***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKuypersAlthouse2009225–245_5-0) [***b***](#cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKuypersAlthouse2009225–245_5-1) [Kuypers & Althouse 2009](#CITEREFKuypersAlthouse2009), pp.\\xa0225–245.\\n6. **[^](#cite_ref-6)** M. [Hebrew](/wiki/Hebrew_scripture \"Hebrew scripture\")) [scripture](/wiki/Scripture \"Scripture\"), argued that civil law arises from [contract](/wiki/Social_contract \"Social contract\") |\\n|  | |\\n\\n**John Selden** (16 December 1584 – 30 November 1654) was an English [jurist](/wiki/Jurist \"Jurist\"), a scholar of England\\'s ancient laws and constitution[[1]](#cite_note-1) and scholar of Jewish law.[[2]](#cite_note-2) He was known as a [polymath](/wiki/Polymath \"Polymath\"); [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton \"John Milton\") hailed Selden in 1644 as \"the chief of learned men reputed in this land\".[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-naturall-4)\\n\\nEarly life\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: Early life\")]\\n\\nHe was born at [Salvington](/wiki/Salvington \"Salvington\"), in the parish of [West Tarring](/wiki/Tarring,_West_Sussex \"Tarring, West Sussex\"), West Sussex (now part of the town of [Worthing](/wiki/Worthing \"Worthing\")), and was baptised at [St Andrew\\'s](/wiki/St_Andrew%27s_Church,_West_Tarring \"St Andrew\\'s Church, West Tarring\"), the [parish church](/wiki/Parish_church \"Parish church\"). The cottage in which he was born survived until 1959 when it was destroyed by a fire caused by an electrical fault.[[5]](#cite_note-WAPH168-5)\\n\\nHis father, also named John Selden, had a small farm. It is said that his skill as a violin-player was what attracted his wife, Margaret, who was from a better family, being the only child of Thomas Baker of [Rustington](/wiki/Rustington \"Rustington\") and descended from a knightly family of [Kent](/wiki/Kent \"Kent\"). Selden was educated at the free grammar school at [Chichester](/wiki/Chichester \"Chichester\"), [The Prebendal School](/wiki/The_Prebendal_School \"The Prebendal School\"),[[6]](#cite_note-6) and in 1600 he went on to [Hart Hall](/wiki/Hertford_College,_Oxford \"Hertford College, Oxford\"), [Oxford](/wiki/University_of_Oxford \"University of Oxford\"). In 1603, he was admitted to [Clifford\\'s Inn](/wiki/Clifford%27s_Inn \"Clifford\\'s Inn\"), London; in 1604 he moved to the [Inner Temple](/wiki/Inner_Temple \"Inner Temple\"); and in 1612 he was [called to the bar](/wiki/Called_to_the_bar \"Called to the bar\"). His earliest patron was Sir [Robert Bruce Cotton](/wiki/Robert_Bruce_Cotton \"Robert Bruce Cotton\"), the antiquary, who seems to have employed him to copy and summarise some of the parliamentary records then held at the [Tower of London](/wiki/Tower_of_London \"Tower of London\"). For some reason, Selden very rarely practised in court, but his practice in [barristers\\' chambers](/wiki/Barristers%27_chambers \"Barristers\\' chambers\") as a conveyancer and consulting counsel was large and apparently lucrative.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nLegal scholar into politics\\n---------------------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Legal scholar into politics\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/John-Selden-David-Wilkins-Joannis-Seldeni-jurisconsulti-Opera_omnia_MG_0668.tif/lossy-page1-250px-John-Selden-David-Wilkins-Joannis-Seldeni-jurisconsulti-Opera_omnia_MG_0668.tif.jpg)](/wiki/File:John-Selden-David-Wilkins-Joannis-Seldeni-jurisconsulti-Opera_omnia_MG_0668.tif)\\n\\nPortrait of Selden (drawn by [Peter Lely](/wiki/Peter_Lely \"Peter Lely\"); engraved by [George Vertue](/wiki/George_Vertue \"George Vertue\")) included in the 1726 edition of his works\\n\\nIn 1618, his *History of Tithes* appeared. Although it had passed censorship and licensing, this dissertation on the historical basis of the [tithe](/wiki/Tithe \"Tithe\") system caused anxiety among the bishops and provoked the intervention of the king, [James I](/wiki/James_VI_and_I \"James VI and I\"). The author was summoned before the [Privy Council](/wiki/Privy_Council_of_England \"Privy Council of England\") and was compelled to retract his opinions.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Also, his work was suppressed, and he was forbidden to reply to anyone who might come forward to answer it.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nThis all seems to have caused Selden\\'s entry into politics. Although he was not in the [Parliament of England](/wiki/Parliament_of_England \"Parliament of England\"), he was the instigator and perhaps the draughtsman of the [Protestation of 1621](/wiki/Protestation_of_1621 \"Protestation of 1621\") on the rights and privileges of the House, affirmed by the [House of Commons](/wiki/British_House_of_Commons \"British House of Commons\") on 18 December 1621. He and several others were imprisoned, at first in the Tower and later under the charge of Sir [Robert Ducie](/wiki/Robert_Ducie \"Robert Ducie\"), [sheriff of London](/wiki/Sheriff_of_London \"Sheriff of London\"). During his brief detention, he occupied himself in preparing an edition of medieval historian [Eadmer](/wiki/Eadmer \"Eadmer\")\\'s *History* from a manuscript lent to him by his host or jailor, which he published two years afterwards.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nParliamentarian\\n---------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section:
