\"Special:EditPage/Template:Marshalsea\") |\\n\\nIn 1623 he was returned to the House of Commons for the [borough](/wiki/Borough \"Borough\") of [Lancaster](/wiki/Lancaster_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Lancaster (UK Parliament constituency)\"), and sat with [John Coke](/wiki/John_Coke \"John Coke\"), [William Noy](/wiki/William_Noy \"William Noy\"), and [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym \"John Pym\") on Sergeant Glanville\\'s election committee. He was also nominated [reader](/wiki/Reader_(Inns_of_Court) \"Reader (Inns of Court)\") of [Lyon\\'s Inn](/wiki/Lyon%27s_Inn \"Lyon\\'s Inn\"), an office he declined to undertake. For this the benchers of the Inner Temple fined him £20 and disqualified him from being one of their number. Nevertheless, after a few years, he became a [master](/wiki/Master_(judiciary) \"Master (judiciary)\") of the bench. In the first parliament of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\") (1625), it appears from the \"returns of members\" printed in 1878 that contrary to the assertion of all his biographers, he had no seat. In Charles\\'s second parliament (1626), he was elected for [Great Bedwyn](/wiki/Great_Bedwyn_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Great Bedwyn (UK Parliament constituency)\") in Wiltshire, and took a prominent part in the impeachment of [George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham](/wiki/George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of_Buckingham \"George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham\"). In the following year, in [Darnell\\'s Case](/wiki/Darnell%27s_Case \"Darnell\\'s Case\") (the Five Knights\\' Case), he was counsel for [Sir Edmund Hampden](/wiki/Sir_Edmund_Hampden \"Sir Edmund Hampden\") in the [Court of King\\'s Bench](/wiki/Court_of_King%27s_Bench_(England) \"Court of King\\'s Bench (England)\").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nIn 1628 he was returned to the third parliament of Charles for [Ludgershall](/wiki/Ludgershall_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Ludgershall (UK Parliament constituency)\"), Wiltshire, and was involved in drawing up and carrying the [Petition of Right](/wiki/Petition_of_Right \"Petition of Right\"). In the session of 1629 he was one of the members responsible for the tumultuous passage in the House of Commons of the resolution against the illegal levy of [tonnage](/wiki/Tonnage \"Tonnage\") and poundage, and, along with Sir [John Eliot](/wiki/John_Eliot_(statesman) \"John Eliot (statesman)\"), [Denzil Holles](/wiki/Denzil_Holles,_1st_Baron_Holles \"Denzil Holles, 1st Baron Holles\"), Long, Valentine, [William Strode](/wiki/William_Strode \"William Strode\"), and the rest, he was sent back to the Tower. There he remained for eight months, deprived for a part of the time of the use of books and writing materials. He was then removed, under less rigorous conditions, to the [Marshalsea](/wiki/Marshalsea \"Marshalsea\"), until [Archbishop Laud](/wiki/William_Laud \"William Laud\") arranged for him to be freed. Some years before, he had been appointed [steward](/wiki/Steward_(office) \"Steward (office)\") to [Henry Grey, 8th Earl of Kent](/wiki/Henry_Grey,_8th_Earl_of_Kent \"Henry Grey, 8th Earl of Kent\"), to whose seat, [Wrest](/wiki/Wrest \"Wrest\") in Bedfordshire, he now retired.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nHe was not elected to the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament \"Short Parliament\") of 1640; but to the [Long Parliament](/wiki/Long_Parliament \"Long Parliament\"), summoned in the autumn, he was returned without opposition for [Oxford University](/wiki/Oxford_University_(UK_Parliament_constituency) \"Oxford University (UK Parliament constituency)\"). He opposed the resolution against [episcopacy](/wiki/Episcopacy \"Episcopacy\") which led to the exclusion of the bishops from the [House of Lords](/wiki/House_of_Lords \"House of Lords\"), and printed an answer to the arguments used by [Sir Harbottle Grimston](/wiki/Sir_Harbottle_Grimston,_1st_Baronet \"Sir Harbottle Grimston, 1st Baronet\") on that occasion. He joined in the protestation of the Commons for the maintenance of the [Protestant](/wiki/Protestant \"Protestant\") religion according to the doctrines of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\"), the authority of the Crown, and the liberty of the subject. He was equally opposed to the court on the question of the commissions of lieutenancy of array and to the parliament on the question of the militia ordinance.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9) In the end, he supported Parliament against King Charles, because, according to him, Charles was certainly acting illegally; but Selden was not certain if Parliament was doing the same.[[10]](#cite_note-10)\\n\\nIn 1643 he participated in the discussions of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly \"Westminster Assembly\"), where his [Erastian](/wiki/Erastian \"Erastian\") views were opposed by [George Gillespie](/wiki/George_Gillespie \"George Gillespie\").[[11]](#cite_note-11) Selden\\'s allies included [Thomas Coleman](/wiki/Thomas_Coleman \"Thomas Coleman\"), [John Lightfoot](/wiki/John_Lightfoot \"John Lightfoot\"), and [Bulstrode Whitelocke](/wiki/Bulstrode_Whitelocke \"Bulstrode Whitelocke\").[[12]](#cite_note-12)\\n\\nIn October 1643 Selden was appointed by Commons to take control of the office of Clerk and Keeper of the Records in the Tower, which duty passed to the Master of the Rolls in 1651.[[13]](#cite_note-13) In 1645, he was named one of the parliamentary commissioners of the [admiralty](/wiki/British_Admiralty \"British Admiralty\") and was elected master of [Trinity Hall, Cambridge](/wiki/Trinity_Hall,_Cambridge \"Trinity Hall, Cambridge\"), an office that he declined to accept. In 1646, he subscribed to the [Solemn League and Covenant](/wiki/Solemn_League_and_Covenant \"Solemn League and Covenant\") and, in 1647, was voted [£](/wiki/GBP \"GBP\")5000 (£898,000 in 2023[[14]](#cite_note-inflation-UK-14)) by the parliament as compensation for his pains under the monarchy.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9)\\n\\nLast years\\n----------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: Last years\")]\\n\\nAfter the death of the [Earl of Kent](/wiki/Henry_Grey,_8th_Earl_of_Kent \"Henry Grey, 8th Earl of Kent\") in 1639, Selden lived permanently under the same roof with the earl\\'s widow, the former [Elizabeth Talbot](/wiki/Elizabeth_Grey,_Countess_of_Kent \"Elizabeth Grey, Countess of Kent\"). It is believed that he married her, although their marriage does not seem to have ever been publicly acknowledged.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9) He assembled a famous library which eventually became part of the [Bodleian Library](/wiki/Bodleian_Library \"Bodleian Library\")\\'s collection in 1659. In addition to a wide range of Greek, Arabic, Hebrew and Latin works, it included the [Codex Mendoza](/wiki/Codex_Mendoza \"Codex Mendoza\") and the [Selden Map of China](/wiki/Selden_Map_of_China \"Selden Map of China\").[[15]](#cite_note-15) He died at Friary House in [Whitefriars](/wiki/Whitefriars,_London \"Whitefriars, London\"), London on 30 November 1654, and was buried in the [Temple Church](/wiki/Temple_Church \"Temple Church\"), London. His tomb is today clearly visible through glass plates in the floor of this church. Furthermore, he is commemorated by a monumental inscription on the south side of the Temple Church. More than two centuries after his death, in 1880, a brass tablet was erected to his memory by the benchers of the [Inner Temple](/wiki/Inner_Temple \"Inner Temple\") in the parish church of St. Andrew\\'s, West Tarring.\\n\\nWorks\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Works\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/ONL_%281887%29_1.144_-_Plan_of_Fleet_Street%2C_the_Temple%2C_etc%2C_1563.jpg/250px-ONL_%281887%29_1.144_-_Plan_of_Fleet_Street%2C_the_Temple%2C_etc%2C_1563.jpg)](/wiki/File:ONL_(1887)_1.144_-_Plan_of_Fleet_Street,_the_Temple,_etc,_1563.jpg)\\n\\nPlan of the Temple as Selden would have known it, based on the \"[Woodcut map of London](/wiki/Woodcut_map_of_London \"Woodcut map of London\")\" of the early 1560s\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/John_Selden_and_his_table-talk_%28IA_cu31924013123108%29.pdf/page1-250px-John_Selden_and_his_table-talk_%28IA_cu31924013123108%29.pdf.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Selden_and_his_table-talk_(IA_cu31924013123108).pdf)\\n\\n1899 edition of Selden\\'s *Table Talk* by [Robert Waters](/wiki/Robert_Waters \"Robert Waters\") (1835–1910)\\n\\nIt was as a prolific scholar and writer that Selden won his reputation. The early books were on English history.\\n\\n### English history and antiquities\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: English history and antiquities\")]\\n\\nIn 1610 three of his works came out: *Jani Anglorum Facies Altera* (*The Back Face* [or *Two Faces*] *of the English [Janus](/wiki/Janus \"Janus\")*) and *England\\'s Epinomis*,[[16]](#cite_note-16) which dealt with the progress of English law down to [Henry II](/wiki/Henry_II_of_England \"Henry II of England\"); and *The Duello, or Single Combat*, in which he traced the history of [trial by battle](/wiki/Trial_by_combat \"Trial by combat\") in England from the Norman Conquest. In 1613 he supplied a series of notes, including quotations and references, to the first eighteen [cantos](/wiki/Canto \"Canto\") of [Michael Drayton](/wiki/Michael_Drayton \"Michael Drayton\")\\'s *[Poly-Olbion](/wiki/Poly-Olbion \"Poly-Olbion\")*. In 1614 he published *Titles of Honor*,[[17]](#cite_note-17) which, in spite of defects and omissions, remained a comprehensive work for centuries.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7) It was republished in a larger and greatly revised edition in 1631, and in a third edition in 1672. It earned for Selden the praise \"monarch of letters\" from his friend [Ben Jonson](/wiki/Ben_Jonson \"Ben Jonson\").[[18]](#cite_note-18)\\n\\nIn 1615, the *Analecton Anglobritannicon*, an account of the civil administration of England before the [Norman Conquest](/wiki/Norman_Conquest \"Norman Conquest\"), written in 1607, was published; its title and argument imitated the *[Franco-Gallia](/wiki/Franco-Gallia \"Franco-Gallia\")* of [François Hotman](/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Hotman \"François Hotman\").[[19]](#cite_note-19) In 1616 appeared notes on [John Fortescue](/wiki/John_Fortescue_(judge) \"John Fortescue (judge)\")\\'s *De laudibus legum Angliae* and [Ralph de Hengham](/wiki/Ralph_de_Hengham \"Ralph de Hengham\")\\'s *Summae magna et parva*.[[20]](#cite_note-20)\\n\\nIn 1618 his controversial *History of Tithes* was published. A first sign of the coming storm was the 1619 book controverting Selden, *Sacrilege Sacredly Handled in two parts; with an Appendix, answering some objections* by [James Sempill](/wiki/James_Sempill \"James Sempill\").[[21]](#cite_note-21) Selden hit back, but was soon gagged. The churchmen [Richard Tillesley](/wiki/Richard_Tillesley \"Richard Tillesley\") (1582–1621) (*Animadversions upon M. Seldens History of Tithes*, 1619) and [Richard Montagu](/wiki/Richard_Montagu \"Richard Montagu\") (*Diatribae upon the first part of the late History of Tithes*, 1621) attacked the work.[[22]](#cite_note-22) There were further replies by [William Sclater](/wiki/William_Sclater_(priest) \"William Sclater (priest)\") (*The Quaestion of Tythes Revised*, 1623), and by [Stephen Nettles](/wiki/Stephen_Nettles \"Stephen Nettles\") (*Answer to the Jewish Part of Mr. Selden\\'s History of Tithes* 1625). In it Selden tried to demonstrate that tithing depended on the civil law, rather than [canon law](/wiki/Canon_law \"Canon law\"). He also made much of the complexities of the ancient Jewish customs on tithes.[[23]](#cite_note-23)\\nThe work was also a milestone in the history of English historical writing through its mixture of [antiquarian](/wiki/Antiquarian \"Antiquarian\")-philological scholarship with historical narrative, two approaches to the study of the past previously seen as distinct.\\n\\nIn 1623 he produced an edition of [Eadmer](/wiki/Eadmer \"Eadmer\")\\'s *Historia Novarum*. It was notable for including in appendices information from the *[Domesday Book](/wiki/Domesday_Book \"Domesday Book\")*, which at the time had not been published and could only be consulted in the original at Westminster, on the payment of a fee.[[24]](#cite_note-24)\\n\\nHe published in 1642 *Privileges of the Baronage of England when they sit in Parliament and Discourse concerning the Rights and Privileges of the Subject*. In 1652 he wrote a preface and collated some of the manuscripts for [Sir Roger Twysden\\'s](/wiki/Roger_Twysden \"Roger Twysden\") *Historiae Anglicanae scriptores X*.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/John_Selden%2C_Tracts_Written_by_John_Selden_of_the_Inner-Temple%2C_Esquire_%281st_ed%2C_1683%2C_title_page%29.jpg/250px-John_Selden%2C_Tracts_Written_by_John_Selden_of_the_Inner-Temple%2C_Esquire_%281st_ed%2C_1683%2C_title_page%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Selden,_Tracts_Written_by_John_Selden_of_the_Inner-Temple,_Esquire_(1st_ed,_1683,_title_page).jpg)\\n\\n*Tracts*, published posthumously in 1683, contained English translations\\n\\n### Literature and archaeology of the Near East\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=7 \"Edit section: Literature and archaeology of the Near East\")]\\n\\nIn 1617, his *De dis Syris* was issued, and immediately established his fame as an orientalist. It is remarkable for its early use of the comparative method, on [Semitic mythology](/wiki/Semitic_mythology \"Semitic mythology\").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7) Also, in 1642, he published a part of the Arabic chronicle of [Patriarch Eutychius of Alexandria](/wiki/Patriarch_Eutychius_of_Alexandria \"Patriarch Eutychius of Alexandria\"), under the title *Eutychii Aegyptii, Patriarchae Orthodoxorum Alexandrini, ... ecclesiae suae origines*. Controversial was the discussion in it of the absence in Alexandria of the distinction between priests and bishops, a burning issue in the debate at the time in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England \"Church of England\").[[25]](#cite_note-25)\\n\\nIn 1628, at the suggestion of Sir Robert Cotton, Selden compiled, with the assistance of two other scholars, [Patrick Young](/wiki/Patrick_Young \"Patrick Young\") and [Richard James](/wiki/Richard_James_(scholar) \"Richard James (scholar)\"), a catalogue of the [Arundel marbles](/wiki/Arundel_marbles \"Arundel marbles\").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\n### Studies on Judaism\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=8 \"Edit section: Studies on Judaism\")]\\n\\nHe employed his leisure at Wrest in writing *De successionibus in bona defuncti secundum leges Ebraeorum* and *De successione in pontificatum Ebraeorum*, published in 1631.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nDuring the progress of the constitutional conflict, he was absorbed in research, publishing *De jure naturali et gentium juxta disciplinam Ebraeorum* in 1640.[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600–601-26) It was a contribution to the theorising of the period on [natural law](/wiki/Natural_law \"Natural law\"). In the words of [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton \"John Milton\"), this \"volume of naturall & national laws proves, not only by great authorities brought together, but by exquisite reasons and theorems almost mathematically demonstrative, that all opinions, yea errors, known, read, and collated, are of main service & assistance toward the speedy attainment of what is truest.\"[[4]](#cite_note-naturall-4)[[27]](#cite_note-27) It develops into a theory of [international law](/wiki/International_law \"International law\"), taking as its basis the [Seven Laws of Noah](/wiki/Seven_Laws_of_Noah \"Seven Laws of Noah\").[[28]](#cite_note-28)\\n\\nIn 1644, he published *Dissertatio de anno civili et calendario reipublicae Judaicae*, in 1646 his treatise on marriage and divorce among the Jews entitled *Uxor Ebraica*, and in 1647 the earliest printed edition of the old English law-book *[Fleta](/wiki/Fleta \"Fleta\")*. In 1650 Selden began to print the trilogy he planned on the [Sanhedrin](/wiki/Sanhedrin \"Sanhedrin\"), as the first part of *De synedriis et prefecturis juridicis veterum Ebraeorum* through the press, the second and third parts being severally published in 1653 and 1655.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9) The aim of this work was to counter the use by the Presbyterians, in particular, of arguments and precedents drawn from Jewish tradition; it was a very detailed study aimed at refuting such arguments, and pointing out the inherent flexibility of the tradition that was being cited.[[29]](#cite_note-29)\\n\\n### International law\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=9 \"Edit section: International law\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/John_Selden_from_NPG_%282%29_cleaned.jpg/250px-John_Selden_from_NPG_%282%29_cleaned.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Selden_from_NPG_(2)_cleaned.jpg)\\n\\nA portrait of John Selden held by the [National Portrait Gallery, London](/wiki/National_Portrait_Gallery,_London \"National Portrait Gallery, London\")\\n\\nHis *[Mare clausum](/wiki/Mare_clausum \"Mare clausum\")* was written to dismantle the pretensions advanced by [Grotius](/wiki/Hugo_Grotius \"Hugo Grotius\") in *[The Free Sea](/wiki/The_Free_Sea \"The Free Sea\")* (*Mare liberum*), on behalf of the Dutch fishermen, to poach in the waters off the English coasts.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nThe circumstances of its delayed publication, in 1635, suggest that during the early 1630s Selden inclined towards the court rather than the popular party and even secured the personal favour of the king, [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England \"Charles I of England\"). It had been written sixteen or seventeen years earlier, but for political reasons Charles\\'s predecessor, [James I](/wiki/James_I_of_England \"James I of England\"), had prohibited its publication. When it eventually appeared, a quarter of a century after *Mare liberum*, it was under Charles\\'s royal patronage, as a kind of state paper, and with a dedication to him. The fact that Selden was not retained in the great case of [ship money](/wiki/Ship_money \"Ship money\") in 1637 by [John Hampden](/wiki/John_Hampden \"John Hampden\"), the cousin of Sir Edmund, his former client in the Five Knights\\' Case, may be taken as additional evidence that his zeal for the popular cause was neither so warm nor so unquestioned as it had once been.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911600-7)\\n\\nHis last publication was a vindication of himself from certain charges advanced against him and his *Mare clausum* around 1653 by [Theodore Graswinckel](/wiki/Theodore_Graswinckel \"Theodore Graswinckel\"), a Dutch jurist.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9)\\n\\n### Posthumous publications\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=10 \"Edit section: Posthumous publications\")]\\n\\nSeveral of Selden\\'s minor works were printed for the first time after his death, including a tract in defence of the 25 December birth of Christ written during the Puritan Commonwealth (1649–1660) when celebration of Christmas was prohibited.[[30]](#cite_note-30) A collective edition of his writings was published by [David Wilkins](/wiki/David_Wilkins_(archdeacon) \"David Wilkins (archdeacon)\") in 3 volumes folio in 1725, and again in 1726. *Table Talk*, for which he is perhaps best known, did not appear until 1689. It was edited by his [amanuensis](/wiki/Amanuensis \"Amanuensis\"), [Richard Milward](/wiki/Richard_Milward_(priest) \"Richard Milward (priest)\"), who affirms that \"the sense and notion is wholly Selden\\'s\" and that \"most of the words\" are his also. Its genuineness has sometimes been questioned.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911601-9)\\n\\nViews\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=11 \"Edit section: Views\")]\\n\\nSelden arrived at an [Erastian](/wiki/Erastian \"Erastian\") position in church politics. He also believed in [free will](/wiki/Free_will \"Free will\"), which was inconsistent with [Calvinism](/wiki/Calvinism \"Calvinism\").[[31]](#cite_note-31)\\n\\nHe was sceptical of the legend of [King Arthur](/wiki/King_Arthur \"King Arthur\") as it had grown up, but believed Arthur had existed.[[32]](#cite_note-32) The [Druids](/wiki/Druids \"Druids\"), he suggested in comments on *Poly-Olbion*, were ancient and presumed esoteric thinkers.[[33]](#cite_note-33) The popular image of a Druid descends via a masque of [Inigo Jones](/wiki/Inigo_Jones \"Inigo Jones\") from a reconstruction by Selden, based (without good foundations) on ancient German statuary.[[34]](#cite_note-34)\\n\\nCommemoration\\n-------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=12 \"Edit section: Commemoration\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Selden_Soc_vols.jpg/500px-Selden_Soc_vols.jpg)](/wiki/File:Selden_Soc_vols.jpg)\\n\\nVolumes published by the [Selden Society](/wiki/Selden_Society \"Selden Society\")\\n\\nSelden is commemorated in the name of the [Selden Society](/wiki/Selden_Society \"Selden Society\"), a [learned society](/wiki/Learned_society \"Learned society\") concerned with the study of English legal history, founded in 1887.\\n\\nHe is also commemorated in place-names in Salvington, including \"The John Selden Inn\", which purports to be on the site of his dwelling; Selden Road; and the Selden medical centre. Also The Selden Arms on Lyndhurst Road in Worthing.\\n\\nInfluence\\n---------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=13 \"Edit section: Influence\")]\\n\\nAccording to the *Encyclopedia of Historians and Historical Writing*, he \"played a role of fundamental importance in the transition of English historical writing from a medieval antiquarianism to a more modern understanding of the scope and function of history than had ever before been expressed in Renaissance England\".[[35]](#cite_note-35) His reputation lasted well, with [Mark Pattison](/wiki/Mark_Pattison_(academic) \"Mark Pattison (academic)\") calling him \"the most learned man, not only of his party, but of Englishmen\".[[36]](#cite_note-36)\\n\\nBy about 1640, Selden\\'s views (with those of Grotius) had a large impact on the [Great Tew circle](/wiki/Great_Tew_circle \"Great Tew circle\") around [Lucius Cary, 2nd Viscount Falkland](/wiki/Lucius_Cary,_2nd_Viscount_Falkland \"Lucius Cary, 2nd Viscount Falkland\"): [William Chillingworth](/wiki/William_Chillingworth \"William Chillingworth\"), [Dudley Digges](/wiki/Dudley_Digges \"Dudley Digges\"), [Henry Hammond](/wiki/Henry_Hammond \"Henry Hammond\").[[37]](#cite_note-37) It was in this milieu that Selden met and befriended [Thomas Hobbes](/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes \"Thomas Hobbes\"). They had much in common, in political thought, but the precise connections have not been clarified.[[38]](#cite_note-38)\\n\\n[Richard Cumberland](/wiki/Richard_Cumberland_(philosopher) \"Richard Cumberland (philosopher)\") followed Selden over both Grotius and Hobbes on natural law. Selden contested the scholastic position, after [Cicero](/wiki/Cicero \"Cicero\"), that \"right reason\" could by its dictates alone generate [obligation](/wiki/Moral_obligation \"Moral obligation\"), by claiming that a formal obligation required a superior in authority. In his *De legibus* Cumberland rejects Selden\\'s solution by means of the Noahide laws, in *De jure naturali*, in favour of Selden\\'s less developed alternate solution. The latter is more orthodox for a [Thomist](/wiki/Thomist \"Thomist\"), an *intellectus agens* as a natural faculty in the rational soul, by the mediation of which divine intellect can intervene directly with individuals.[[39]](#cite_note-39) [Matthew Hale](/wiki/Matthew_Hale_(jurist) \"Matthew Hale (jurist)\") tried to merge the theory of Grotius on property with Selden\\'s view on obligation.[[40]](#cite_note-40) Cumberland and Hale both belonged to a larger group, followers in a broad sense of Selden, with backgrounds mostly of Cambridge and the law, comprising also [Orlando Bridgeman](/wiki/Sir_Orlando_Bridgeman,_1st_Baronet,_of_Great_Lever \"Sir Orlando Bridgeman, 1st Baronet, of Great Lever\"), [Hezekiah Burton](/wiki/Hezekiah_Burton \"Hezekiah Burton\"), [John Hollings](/wiki/John_Hollings \"John Hollings\"), [Richard Kidder](/wiki/Richard_Kidder \"Richard Kidder\"), [Edward Stillingfleet](/wiki/Edward_Stillingfleet \"Edward Stillingfleet\"), [John Tillotson](/wiki/John_Tillotson \"John Tillotson\"), and [John Wilkins](/wiki/John_Wilkins \"John Wilkins\").[[41]](#cite_note-41)\\n\\n[Giambattista Vico](/wiki/Giambattista_Vico \"Giambattista Vico\") called Grotius, Selden and [Samuel Pufendorf](/wiki/Samuel_Pufendorf \"Samuel Pufendorf\") the \"three princes\" of the \"natural right of the gentes\". He went on to criticise their approach foundationally.[[42]](#cite_note-42) In his *Autobiography* he specifies that they had conflated the natural law of the \"nations\", based on custom, with that of the philosophers, based on human abstractions.[[43]](#cite_note-43) [Isaiah Berlin](/wiki/Isaiah_Berlin \"Isaiah Berlin\") comments on Vico\\'s admiration for Grotius and Selden.[[44]](#cite_note-44)\\n\\nLibrary collections\\n-------------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Selden&action=edit&section=14 \"Edit section: Library collections\")]\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Bodleian_Library_Arch._B_f.69.png/250px-Bodleian_Library_Arch._B_f.69.png)](/wiki/File:Bodleian_Library_Arch._B_f.69.png)\\n\\nTitle page for John Selden\\'s copy of *Sanctos no gosagues no uchi nuqigaqi quan dai ichi* (1591). This was the first book printed with moveable type in Japan. Oxford, Bodleian Library Arch. B f.69: https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/3bdc1c46-9c84-4e64-aa83-b48b4baf2a5f//\\n\\nBy the time of his death in 1654, Selden had accumulated a library of several thousand manuscripts and printed books. Selden\\'s will left his intentions for this library somewhat ambiguous, although the will and [codicil](/wiki/Codicil_(will) \"Codicil (will)\") seem to suggest that he intended to bequeath most of his [Oriental](/wiki/Orient \"Orient\") manuscripts, Greek manuscripts, a Latin manuscript, and his printed [Talmudic](/wiki/Talmud \"Talmud\") and [Rabbinical](/wiki/Rabbinic_literature \"Rabbinic literature\") books to the [Bodleian Library](/wiki/Bodleian_Library \"Bodleian Library\"), Oxford.[[45]](#cite_note-45) There is some evidence to suggest that Selden intended to leave his printed books and historical manuscripts to the [Inner Temple](/wiki/Inner_Temple \"Inner Temple\") but that this transaction did not occur because the Temple did not possess a large enough library.[[46]](#cite_note-46) By 1656, two years after Selden\\'s death, his executors (Edward Heyward, John Vaughan, [Matthew Hale](/wiki/Matthew_Hale_(jurist) \"Matthew Hale (jurist)\"), and Rowland Jewks) were in negotiation with the Bodleian library to transfer Selden\\'s entire collection.[[47]](#cite_note-:0-47) In 1659, the executors stipulated that Selden\\'s manuscripts \"bee forever heerafter kepte together in one distincte pile and body under the name of Mr. Selden’s Library.\" The Bodleian agreed, and the library received Selden\\'s collection in June 1659.[[48]](#cite_note-48)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._c.2_cover.png/250px-Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._c.2_cover.png)](/wiki/File:Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._c.2_cover.png)\\n\\nCover of John Selden\\'s copy of Boccaccio\\'s *Decamerone*. The design on the cover is similar to the Plantagenet crest. Holes from clasps are also visible. Oxford, Bodleian Library S. Seld. c.2: https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/61459688-0512-49e0-a996-a4f0921956b2/\\n\\nSelden\\'s collection was the largest received by the Bodleian in the seventeenth century, comprising around 8,000 items.[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) Even this massive collection did not represent the extent of Selden\\'s library. Duplicates, meaning books the library already owned, were given to [Gloucester Cathedral](/wiki/Gloucester_Cathedral \"Gloucester Cathedral\") library.[[47]](#cite_note-:0-47) A rumour also circulated in the decades after Selden\\'s death that part of his library had remained in London and was destroyed by a fire. The 1704 edition of [Edward Chamberlayne](/wiki/Edward_Chamberlayne \"Edward Chamberlayne\")\\'s *The Present State of England* claimed that a fire at the Inner Temple destroyed \"8 Chests full\" of Selden\\'s manuscripts.[[50]](#cite_note-50) Still, the collection the Bodleian received was large enough that it required several years and multiple librarians to fully catalogue.[[51]](#cite_note-51) Since then, the original collection has been enhanced by further acquisitions, most notably by a group of forty Selden manuscripts purchased by the Bodleian from James Fairhurst in 1947.[[52]](#cite_note-52)[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) The Selden collection at the Bodleian houses more than 400 manuscript volumes taking up more than 40 meters (approx. 130 feet) of shelf space.[[53]](#cite_note-53)[[54]](#cite_note-54) The linguistic range of these manuscripts reflects Selden\\'s interest in eastern and other languages. The languages represented include\\n\\n* Russian\\n  + An incomplete Russian-English vocabulary (MS. Selden Supra 61)\\n  + Samples of Russian [calligraphy](/wiki/Calligraphy \"Calligraphy\") (MS. Arch. Selden A. 72 (5))\\n* Greek\\n  + Astronomical and musical treatises (MS. Arch. Selden B. 17)\\n  + Several Greek versions of the [New Testament](/wiki/New_Testament \"New Testament\") [Gospels](/wiki/Gospel \"Gospel\") (MS. Selden Supra 2, 3, 6, 28–9)\\n* Arabic\\n  + Prayers, meditations, and [Quranic](/wiki/Quran \"Quran\") praises (MS. Selden Superius 3)\\n  + Works on [astrology](/wiki/Astrology \"Astrology\") and medicine (MS. Selden Superius 15)\\n  + Works on [Algebra](/wiki/Algebra \"Algebra\") and mathematics (MS. Selden Superius 65)\\n* Hebrew\\n  + [Hebrew](/wiki/Hebrew_language \"Hebrew language\") and [Arabic](/wiki/Arabic \"Arabic\") grammar and vocabulary (MS. Selden Supra 107)\\n  + [Kabbalah](/wiki/Kabbalah \"Kabbalah\") and Kabbalistic collections (MS. Arch. Selden A. 56; MS. Selden Superius 107)\\n* New World languages\\n  + A treatise on Mexican hieroglyphics (MS. Arch. Selden A. 2)\\n\\nMany manuscripts relate to Selden\\'s study of the law both in England and internationally. These include\\n\\n* A fragment on Islamic law (MS. Selden Superius 42)\\n* [Canon law](/wiki/Canon_law \"Canon law\") (MS. Arch. Selden A. 63)\\n* An account of the laws of [Ivan the Terrible](/wiki/Ivan_the_Terrible \"Ivan the Terrible\") (MS. Selden Supra. 59)\\n* Various legal topics, such as maritime law and a Latin treatise on procedure in Civil Courts (MS. Arch. Selden B. 27)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._e.2.png/250px-Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._e.2.png)](/wiki/File:Bodleian_Library_S._Seld._e.2.png)\\n\\nA heavily annotated page in John Selden\\'s copy of Aristotle\\'s *Nicomachean Ethics*, translated by Leonardus Brunus Aretinus (1479). The page includes a space left for an [initial](/wiki/Initial \"Initial\") (also called a drop cap). Oxford, Bodleian Library S. Seld. e.2: https://digital.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/objects/032cc92a-b24c-48ab-9c58-3545cf24121f/.\\n\\nSome manuscripts touch on contemporary events. For instance MS. Arch. Selden B. 8 includes a Latin speech given in Oxford on the return of [Prince Charles from Spain in 1623](/wiki/Spanish_match \"Spanish match\"). Still others contain classical works of philosophy and literature, such as\\n\\n* Treatises of Aristotle (MS. Selden Supra 24)\\n* [Aeschylus](/wiki/Aeschylus \"Aeschylus\") and [Lycophron](/wiki/Lycophron \"Lycophron\") (MS. Selden Supra 18)\\n\\nBeyond manuscripts, the Selden collection contains several notable printed works. Among them is the first book ever printed in Japan using moveable type, *Sanctos no gosagueo no uchi nuqigaqi* (Arch.b.f.69).[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) The printed books included in the Selden collection contain many that are significant in part because they originated in the libraries of other famous figures, including [Sir Robert Cotton](/wiki/Sir_Robert_Cotton,_1st_Baronet,_of_Connington \"Sir Robert Cotton, 1st Baronet, of Connington\"), [John Donne](/wiki/John_Donne \"John Donne\"), and [John Dee](/wiki/John_Dee \"John Dee\").[[49]](#cite_note-:1-49) According to [Geoffrey Keynes](/wiki/Geoffrey_Keynes \"Geoffrey Keynes\"), several of the books Selden received from John Donne\\'s library include inscriptions from both men. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

English churchman, rabbinical scholar (1602–1675)

This article is about 17th-century clergyman. For the 18th-century biologist, see [John Lightfoot (biologist)](/wiki/John_Lightfoot_(biologist) "John Lightfoot (biologist)"). For the 19th-century clergyman, see [John Prideaux Lightfoot](/wiki/John_Prideaux_Lightfoot "John Prideaux Lightfoot").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/John_Lightfoot.jpg/250px-John_Lightfoot.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Lightfoot.jpg)

John Lightfoot

**John Lightfoot** (29 March 1602 – 6 December 1675) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") churchman, rabbinical scholar, Vice-Chancellor of the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") and Master of [St Catharine's College, Cambridge](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge").

Life
----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Lightfoot&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

He was born in [Stoke-on-Trent](/wiki/Stoke-on-Trent "Stoke-on-Trent"), the son of Thomas Lightfoot, vicar of [Uttoxeter](/wiki/Uttoxeter "Uttoxeter"), [Staffordshire](/wiki/Staffordshire "Staffordshire"). He was educated at Morton Green near [Congleton](/wiki/Congleton "Congleton"), [Cheshire](/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"), and at [Christ's College, Cambridge](/wiki/Christ%27s_College,_Cambridge "Christ's College, Cambridge"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) where he was regarded as the best [orator](/wiki/Orator "Orator") among the undergraduates. After taking his degree he became assistant master at [Repton School](/wiki/Repton_School "Repton School") in [Derbyshire](/wiki/Derbyshire "Derbyshire"); after taking orders, he was appointed curate of "Norton-under-Hales" (i.e. [Norton in Hales](/wiki/Norton_in_Hales "Norton in Hales")) in [Shropshire](/wiki/Shropshire "Shropshire"). There he attracted the notice of Sir [Rowland Cotton](/wiki/Rowland_Cotton "Rowland Cotton"), an amateur [Hebraist](/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"), who made him his domestic chaplain at Bellaport. Shortly after the removal of Sir Rowland to [London](/wiki/London "London"), Lightfoot, abandoning an intention to go abroad, accepted a charge at [Stone, Staffordshire](/wiki/Stone,_Staffordshire "Stone, Staffordshire"), where he continued for about two years. From Stone he removed to [Hornsey](/wiki/Hornsey "Hornsey"), near London, for the sake of reading in the library of [Sion College](/wiki/Sion_College "Sion College").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In September 1630 he was presented by Cotton to the rectory of [Ashley, Staffordshire](/wiki/Ashley,_Staffordshire "Ashley, Staffordshire"), where he remained until June 1642. He then went to London, probably to supervise the publication of his work, *A Few and New Observations upon the Book of Genesis: the most of them certain; the rest, probable; all, harmless, strange and rarely heard of before*. Soon after his arrival in London he became minister of St Bartholomew's Church, near the Exchange.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Lightfoot was one of the original members of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"); his "Journal of the Proceedings of the Assembly of Divines from January 1, 1643 to December 31, 1644" is a valuable historical source for the brief period to which it relates. He was assiduous in his attendance, and, though frequently standing alone, especially in the [Erastian controversy](/wiki/Erastianism "Erastianism"), he exercised considerable influence on the outcome of the discussions of the Assembly.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

He was made Master of [Catharine Hall](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge") (renamed [St Catharine's College](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge")) by the parliamentary visitors of Cambridge in 1643, and also, on the recommendation of the Assembly, was promoted to the rectory of [Much Munden](/wiki/Great_Munden "Great Munden"), [Hertfordshire](/wiki/Hertfordshire "Hertfordshire"); he kept both appointments until his death.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In 1654 Lightfoot had been chosen vice-chancellor of the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), but continued to live at Munden, in the rectory of which, as well as in the mastership of [Catharine Hall](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge"), he was confirmed at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

While travelling from Cambridge to [Ely](/wiki/Ely,_England "Ely, England"), where he had been collated in 1668 by Sir [Orlando Bridgeman](/wiki/Sir_Orlando_Bridgeman,_1st_Baronet,_of_Great_Lever "Sir Orlando Bridgeman, 1st Baronet, of Great Lever") to a [prebendal stall](/wiki/Prebendal_stall "Prebendal stall"), he caught a severe cold, and died at Ely.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Lightfoot bequeathed his library of [Old Testament](/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament") books and documents to [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"). It was destroyed in a fire at Harvard in 1764.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Works
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Lightfoot&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Works")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Allegorische_figuur_met_Joodse_man_Titelpagina_voor_John_Lightfoot%2C_Opera_Joannis_Ligtfooti_omnia%2C_1686%2C_RP-P-2016-841.jpg/250px-Allegorische_figuur_met_Joodse_man_Titelpagina_voor_John_Lightfoot%2C_Opera_Joannis_Ligtfooti_omnia%2C_1686%2C_RP-P-2016-841.jpg)](/wiki/File:Allegorische_figuur_met_Joodse_man_Titelpagina_voor_John_Lightfoot,_Opera_Joannis_Ligtfooti_omnia,_1686,_RP-P-2016-841.jpg)

John Lightfoot. *Opera omnia*. Rotterdam: [Reinier Leers](/wiki/Reinier_Leers "Reinier Leers"), 1686.

His first published work, entitled *Erubhin*, or *Miscellanies, Christian and Judaical*, written in his spare time and dedicated to Cotton, appeared in London in 1629.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In 1643 Lightfoot published *A Handful of Gleanings out of the Book of Exodus*. Also in 1643 he was appointed to preach the sermon before the [House of Commons](/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England "House of Commons of England") on occasion of the public fast of 29 March. It was published under the title of *Elias Redivivus*, the text being [Luke 1:17](https://www.esv.org/Luke+1:17); in it a parallel is drawn between the [John the Baptist](/wiki/John_the_Baptist "John the Baptist")'s ministry and the work of reformation which in the preacher's judgment was incumbent on the [Parliament](/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") of his own day.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In 1644 the first instalment of an unfinished work was published in London. The full title was *The Harmony of the Four Evangelists among themselves, and with the Old Testament, with an explanation of the chiefest difficulties both in Language and Sense: Part I. From the beginning of the Gospels to the Baptism of our Saviour*. The second part, *From the Baptism of our Saviour to the first Passover after*, followed in 1647, and the third, *From the first Passover after our Saviour's Baptism to the second*, in 1650. On 26 August 1645 he again preached before the [House of Commons](/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England "House of Commons of England") on the day of their monthly fast. His text was [Revelation 20:1–2](https://www.esv.org/Revelation+20:1).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In these books he dated Creation to 3929 BC (see [Ussher chronology](/wiki/Ussher_chronology#Lightfoot's_Creation "Ussher chronology")). Understanding of Lightfoot's precise meaning has been complicated by an 1896 misquotation of him cited by [Andrew Dickson White](/wiki/Andrew_Dickson_White "Andrew Dickson White").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Rejecting the doctrine of the [millenarian](/wiki/Millenarianism "Millenarianism") sects, Lightfoot had various practical suggestions for the repression of current "blasphemies", for a thorough revision of the [Authorized Version](/wiki/Authorized_Version "Authorized Version") of the Scriptures (*On a fresh revision of the English New Testament*), for the encouragement of a learned ministry, and for a speedy settlement of the church. *A Commentary upon the Acts of the Apostles, ironic and critical; the Difficulties of the text explained, and the times of the Story cast into annals. From the beginning of the Book to the end of the Twelfth Chapter. With a brief survey of the contemporary Story of the Jews and Romans (down to the third year of Claudius)* was published later that year. In 1647 came *The Harmony, Chronicle, and Order of the Old Testament*, followed in 1655 by *The Harmony, Chronicle, and Order of the New Testament*, inscribed to [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

He helped [Brian Walton](/wiki/Brian_Walton_(bishop) "Brian Walton (bishop)") with the *[Polyglot Bible](/wiki/Polyglot_Bible "Polyglot Bible")* (1657). His own best-known work was the *Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae*, in which the volume relating to the [Gospel of Matthew](/wiki/Gospel_of_Matthew "Gospel of Matthew") appeared in 1658, that relating to the [Gospel of Mark](/wiki/Gospel_of_Mark "Gospel of Mark") in 1663, and those relating to [1 Corinthians](/wiki/1_Corinthians "1 Corinthians"), [John](/wiki/Gospel_of_John "Gospel of John"), and [Luke](/wiki/Gospel_of_Luke "Gospel of Luke"), in 1664, 1671, and 1674 respectively.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The *Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae impensae in Acta Apostolorum et in Ep. S. Pauli ad Romanos* were published posthumously.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Editions
--------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Lightfoot&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Editions")]

The *Works of Lightfoot* were first edited, in 2 vols. fol., by George Bright and [John Strype](/wiki/John_Strype "John Strype") in 1684.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The *Opera Omnia, cura Joh. Texelii*, appeared at Rotterdam in 1686 (2 vols. fol.), and again, edited by [Johann Leusden](/wiki/Johann_Leusden "Johann Leusden"), at Franeker in 1699 (3 vols. 101.). A volume of *Remains* was published at London in 1700.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The *Hor. Hebr. et Talm.* were also edited in [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") by [Johann Benedict Carpzov](/wiki/Johann_Benedict_Carpzov "Johann Benedict Carpzov") (Leipzig, 1675–1679), and again, in English, by [Robert Gandell](/wiki/Robert_Gandell "Robert Gandell") (Oxford, 1859).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The most complete edition is that of the *Whole Works*, in 13 vols. 8vo. edited, with a life, by [John Rogers Pitman](/wiki/John_Rogers_Pitman "John Rogers Pitman") (London, 1822–1825). It includes, besides the works already noticed, numerous sermons, letters and miscellaneous writings; and also *The Temple, especially as it stood in the Days of our Saviour* (London, 1650).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

English churchman, rabbinical scholar (1602–1675)

This article is about 17th-century clergyman. For the 18th-century biologist, see [John Lightfoot (biologist)](/wiki/John_Lightfoot_(biologist) "John Lightfoot (biologist)"). For the 19th-century clergyman, see [John Prideaux Lightfoot](/wiki/John_Prideaux_Lightfoot "John Prideaux Lightfoot").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/John_Lightfoot.jpg/250px-John_Lightfoot.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_Lightfoot.jpg)

John Lightfoot

**John Lightfoot** (29 March 1602 – 6 December 1675) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") churchman, rabbinical scholar, Vice-Chancellor of the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") and Master of [St Catharine's College, Cambridge](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge").

Life
----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Lightfoot&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

He was born in [Stoke-on-Trent](/wiki/Stoke-on-Trent "Stoke-on-Trent"), the son of Thomas Lightfoot, vicar of [Uttoxeter](/wiki/Uttoxeter "Uttoxeter"), [Staffordshire](/wiki/Staffordshire "Staffordshire"). He was educated at Morton Green near [Congleton](/wiki/Congleton "Congleton"), [Cheshire](/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"), and at [Christ's College, Cambridge](/wiki/Christ%27s_College,_Cambridge "Christ's College, Cambridge"),[[1]](#cite_note-1) where he was regarded as the best [orator](/wiki/Orator "Orator") among the undergraduates. After taking his degree he became assistant master at [Repton School](/wiki/Repton_School "Repton School") in [Derbyshire](/wiki/Derbyshire "Derbyshire"); after taking orders, he was appointed curate of "Norton-under-Hales" (i.e. [Norton in Hales](/wiki/Norton_in_Hales "Norton in Hales")) in [Shropshire](/wiki/Shropshire "Shropshire"). There he attracted the notice of Sir [Rowland Cotton](/wiki/Rowland_Cotton "Rowland Cotton"), an amateur [Hebraist](/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language"), who made him his domestic chaplain at Bellaport. Shortly after the removal of Sir Rowland to [London](/wiki/London "London"), Lightfoot, abandoning an intention to go abroad, accepted a charge at [Stone, Staffordshire](/wiki/Stone,_Staffordshire "Stone, Staffordshire"), where he continued for about two years. From Stone he removed to [Hornsey](/wiki/Hornsey "Hornsey"), near London, for the sake of reading in the library of [Sion College](/wiki/Sion_College "Sion College").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In September 1630 he was presented by Cotton to the rectory of [Ashley, Staffordshire](/wiki/Ashley,_Staffordshire "Ashley, Staffordshire"), where he remained until June 1642. He then went to London, probably to supervise the publication of his work, *A Few and New Observations upon the Book of Genesis: the most of them certain; the rest, probable; all, harmless, strange and rarely heard of before*. Soon after his arrival in London he became minister of St Bartholomew's Church, near the Exchange.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Lightfoot was one of the original members of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"); his "Journal of the Proceedings of the Assembly of Divines from January 1, 1643 to December 31, 1644" is a valuable historical source for the brief period to which it relates. He was assiduous in his attendance, and, though frequently standing alone, especially in the [Erastian controversy](/wiki/Erastianism "Erastianism"), he exercised considerable influence on the outcome of the discussions of the Assembly.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

He was made Master of [Catharine Hall](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge") (renamed [St Catharine's College](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge")) by the parliamentary visitors of Cambridge in 1643, and also, on the recommendation of the Assembly, was promoted to the rectory of [Much Munden](/wiki/Great_Munden "Great Munden"), [Hertfordshire](/wiki/Hertfordshire "Hertfordshire"); he kept both appointments until his death.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In 1654 Lightfoot had been chosen vice-chancellor of the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge"), but continued to live at Munden, in the rectory of which, as well as in the mastership of [Catharine Hall](/wiki/St_Catharine%27s_College,_Cambridge "St Catharine's College, Cambridge"), he was confirmed at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

While travelling from Cambridge to [Ely](/wiki/Ely,_England "Ely, England"), where he had been collated in 1668 by Sir [Orlando Bridgeman](/wiki/Sir_Orlando_Bridgeman,_1st_Baronet,_of_Great_Lever "Sir Orlando Bridgeman, 1st Baronet, of Great Lever") to a [prebendal stall](/wiki/Prebendal_stall "Prebendal stall"), he caught a severe cold, and died at Ely.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2) Lightfoot bequeathed his library of [Old Testament](/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament") books and documents to [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"). It was destroyed in a fire at Harvard in 1764.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Works
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Lightfoot&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Works")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Allegorische_figuur_met_Joodse_man_Titelpagina_voor_John_Lightfoot%2C_Opera_Joannis_Ligtfooti_omnia%2C_1686%2C_RP-P-2016-841.jpg/250px-Allegorische_figuur_met_Joodse_man_Titelpagina_voor_John_Lightfoot%2C_Opera_Joannis_Ligtfooti_omnia%2C_1686%2C_RP-P-2016-841.jpg)](/wiki/File:Allegorische_figuur_met_Joodse_man_Titelpagina_voor_John_Lightfoot,_Opera_Joannis_Ligtfooti_omnia,_1686,_RP-P-2016-841.jpg)

John Lightfoot. *Opera omnia*. Rotterdam: [Reinier Leers](/wiki/Reinier_Leers "Reinier Leers"), 1686.

His first published work, entitled *Erubhin*, or *Miscellanies, Christian and Judaical*, written in his spare time and dedicated to Cotton, appeared in London in 1629.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In 1643 Lightfoot published *A Handful of Gleanings out of the Book of Exodus*. Also in 1643 he was appointed to preach the sermon before the [House of Commons](/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England "House of Commons of England") on occasion of the public fast of 29 March. It was published under the title of *Elias Redivivus*, the text being [Luke 1:17](https://www.esv.org/Luke+1:17); in it a parallel is drawn between the [John the Baptist](/wiki/John_the_Baptist "John the Baptist")'s ministry and the work of reformation which in the preacher's judgment was incumbent on the [Parliament](/wiki/Parliament_of_England "Parliament of England") of his own day.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In 1644 the first instalment of an unfinished work was published in London. The full title was *The Harmony of the Four Evangelists among themselves, and with the Old Testament, with an explanation of the chiefest difficulties both in Language and Sense: Part I. From the beginning of the Gospels to the Baptism of our Saviour*. The second part, *From the Baptism of our Saviour to the first Passover after*, followed in 1647, and the third, *From the first Passover after our Saviour's Baptism to the second*, in 1650. On 26 August 1645 he again preached before the [House of Commons](/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_England "House of Commons of England") on the day of their monthly fast. His text was [Revelation 20:1–2](https://www.esv.org/Revelation+20:1).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

In these books he dated Creation to 3929 BC (see [Ussher chronology](/wiki/Ussher_chronology#Lightfoot's_Creation "Ussher chronology")). Understanding of Lightfoot's precise meaning has been complicated by an 1896 misquotation of him cited by [Andrew Dickson White](/wiki/Andrew_Dickson_White "Andrew Dickson White").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Rejecting the doctrine of the [millenarian](/wiki/Millenarianism "Millenarianism") sects, Lightfoot had various practical suggestions for the repression of current "blasphemies", for a thorough revision of the [Authorized Version](/wiki/Authorized_Version "Authorized Version") of the Scriptures (*On a fresh revision of the English New Testament*), for the encouragement of a learned ministry, and for a speedy settlement of the church. *A Commentary upon the Acts of the Apostles, ironic and critical; the Difficulties of the text explained, and the times of the Story cast into annals. From the beginning of the Book to the end of the Twelfth Chapter. With a brief survey of the contemporary Story of the Jews and Romans (down to the third year of Claudius)* was published later that year. In 1647 came *The Harmony, Chronicle, and Order of the Old Testament*, followed in 1655 by *The Harmony, Chronicle, and Order of the New Testament*, inscribed to [Oliver Cromwell](/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell "Oliver Cromwell").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

He helped [Brian Walton](/wiki/Brian_Walton_(bishop) "Brian Walton (bishop)") with the *[Polyglot Bible](/wiki/Polyglot_Bible "Polyglot Bible")* (1657). His own best-known work was the *Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae*, in which the volume relating to the [Gospel of Matthew](/wiki/Gospel_of_Matthew "Gospel of Matthew") appeared in 1658, that relating to the [Gospel of Mark](/wiki/Gospel_of_Mark "Gospel of Mark") in 1663, and those relating to [1 Corinthians](/wiki/1_Corinthians "1 Corinthians"), [John](/wiki/Gospel_of_John "Gospel of John"), and [Luke](/wiki/Gospel_of_Luke "Gospel of Luke"), in 1664, 1671, and 1674 respectively.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The *Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae impensae in Acta Apostolorum et in Ep. S. Pauli ad Romanos* were published posthumously.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

Editions
--------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=John_Lightfoot&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Editions")]

The *Works of Lightfoot* were first edited, in 2 vols. fol., by George Bright and [John Strype](/wiki/John_Strype "John Strype") in 1684.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The *Opera Omnia, cura Joh. Texelii*, appeared at Rotterdam in 1686 (2 vols. fol.), and again, edited by [Johann Leusden](/wiki/Johann_Leusden "Johann Leusden"), at Franeker in 1699 (3 vols. 101.). A volume of *Remains* was published at London in 1700.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The *Hor. Hebr. et Talm.* were also edited in [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") by [Johann Benedict Carpzov](/wiki/Johann_Benedict_Carpzov "Johann Benedict Carpzov") (Leipzig, 1675–1679), and again, in English, by [Robert Gandell](/wiki/Robert_Gandell "Robert Gandell") (Oxford, 1859).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

The most complete edition is that of the *Whole Works*, in 13 vols. 8vo. edited, with a life, by [John Rogers Pitman](/wiki/John_Rogers_Pitman "John Rogers Pitman") (London, 1822–1825). It includes, besides the works already noticed, numerous sermons, letters and miscellaneous writings; and also *The Temple, especially as it stood in the Days of our Saviour* (London, 1650).[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-2)

***Apology for Smectymnuus***, or *An Apology for a Pamphlet*, was published by [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in April 1642. It was the final of his [antiprelatical tracts](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts") which criticize the structure of the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

The *[Apology](/wiki/Apologetics "Apologetics")* was published in April 1642 as *An Apology against a Pamphlet Called a Modest Confutation of the Animadversions upon the Remonstrant against Smectymnvvs* and is [his final antiprelatical tract](/wiki/Milton%27s_antiprelatical_tracts "Milton's antiprelatical tracts"). The tract was written as a response to a refutation by Bishop [Joseph Hall](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Milton argues that the defense of truth makes one vulnerable to personal attacks and emphasizes that role of personal integrity, especially his own:[[2]](#cite_note-2) "as a member incorporate into that truth whereof I was perswaded".[[3]](#cite_note-3) Milton defends his own integrity when he later writes:[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) "that indeed according to art is most eloquent, which returns and approaches neerest to nature from whence it came; and they expresse nature best, who in their lives least wander from her safe leading, which may be call'd regenerate reason".[[5]](#cite_note-5) This idea is expanded further when he says:

> he who would not be frustrated of his hope to write well hereafter in laudable things, ought him selfe to bee a true Poem, that is, a composition, and patterne of the best and honourable things; not presuming to sing high praises of heroick men, or famous Cities, unlesse he have in himselfe the experience and the practice of all that which is praise-worthy.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Apology_for_Smectymnuus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

The *Apology*, like many of Milton's other tracts, praises Parliament and emphasizes that they are reformers and the basis of the country.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The tract also connects truth of words with the individual's character.[[4]](#cite_note-Wheeler_p._275-4) Paul Stevens emphasizes that the tract reflects how "Milton's self is produced in the process of writing" and that his self is put through "a series of culturally approved *laterall* transformations".[[8]](#cite_note-8) In particular, Elizabeth Wheeler points out that the tract contains "Milton's understanding of [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle")'s definition of man as a political animal. Heroism lies in the risk of changing and being changed in verbal exchange."[[9]](#cite_note-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Group of clergy active in 1641 England

**Smectymnuus** was the *[nom de plume](/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")* of a group of [Puritan](/wiki/Puritan "Puritan") clergymen active in [England](/wiki/England "England") in 1641 during the reign of [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland "Charles I of England, Scotland, and Ireland"). It comprised four leading English churchmen, and one Scottish minister ([Thomas Young](/wiki/Thomas_Young_(1587-1655) "Thomas Young (1587-1655)")). They went on to provide leadership for the anti-episcopal forces in the [Church of England](/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), continuing into the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly"), where they also opposed the Independent movement.

The name is an acronym derived from the initials of the five authors: [Stephen Marshall](/wiki/Stephen_Marshall_(English_clergyman) "Stephen Marshall (English clergyman)"), [Edmund Calamy](/wiki/Edmund_Calamy_the_Elder "Edmund Calamy the Elder"), Thomas Young, [Matthew Newcomen](/wiki/Matthew_Newcomen "Matthew Newcomen"), and [William Spurstow](/wiki/William_Spurstow "William Spurstow"). Their first pamphlet, *An Answer to a booke entituled, An Humble Remonstrance. In Which, the Original of Liturgy and Episcopacy is discussed*, appeared in March 1641. The pamphlet was written in response to [Joseph Hall's](/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(bishop) "Joseph Hall (bishop)") *An Humble Remonstrance to the High Court of Parliament*. It is thought that [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") wrote the postscript for Smectymnuus's reply.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

This response provoked Hall to write another reply: *A Defence of the Humble Remonstrance, against the Frivolous and false Expectations of Smectymnuus*. Smectymnuus answered Hall again with their *A Vindication of the Answer to the Humble Remonstrance, from the Unjust Imputations of Frivolousnesse and Falsehood*.

Milton also published two tracts defending the Smectymnuus group from Hall: *[Animadversions upon The Remonstrants Defence Against Smectymnvvs](/wiki/Animadversions "Animadversions")* (1641) and *[Apology for Smectymnuus](/wiki/Apology_for_Smectymnuus "Apology for Smectymnuus")* (1642).[[2]](#cite_note-2) Thomas Young was a former tutor and close friend to Milton.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

**Stephen Marshall** (c. 1594 – 1655) was an [English](/wiki/England "England") [Nonconformist](/wiki/Nonconformist_(Protestantism) "Nonconformist (Protestantism)") churchman. His sermons, especially that on the death of [John Pym](/wiki/John_Pym "John Pym") in 1643, reveal eloquence and fervour. The only "systematic" work he published was *A Defence of [Infant Baptism](/wiki/Infant_Baptism "Infant Baptism")*, against [John Tombes](/wiki/John_Tombes "John Tombes") (1646).

Early life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

He was born at [Godmanchester](/wiki/Godmanchester "Godmanchester") in [Huntingdonshire](/wiki/Huntingdonshire "Huntingdonshire"), and was educated at [Emmanuel College, Cambridge](/wiki/Emmanuel_College,_Cambridge "Emmanuel College, Cambridge") (M.A. 1622, B.D. 1629). After holding the living of [Wethersfield](/wiki/Wethersfield,_Essex "Wethersfield, Essex") in [Essex](/wiki/Essex,_England "Essex, England"), he became vicar of [Finchingfield](/wiki/Finchingfield "Finchingfield"). In 1636 he was reported for "want of conformity."

Civil War years
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil War years")]

Marshall was a powerful preacher: [Robert Baillie](/wiki/Robert_Baillie "Robert Baillie") noted that he was reckoned the best in England.[[1]](#cite_note-1) He also influenced the elections for the [Short Parliament](/wiki/Short_Parliament "Short Parliament") of 1640: [Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon](/wiki/Edward_Hyde,_1st_Earl_of_Clarendon "Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon") considered his influence on the parliamentary side to be greater than that of [William Laud](/wiki/William_Laud "William Laud") on the royalist. In 1642 Marshall was appointed lecturer at [St Margaret's, Westminster](/wiki/St._Margaret%27s,_Westminster "St. Margaret's, Westminster"), and delivered a series of addresses to the Commons in which he advocated episcopal and liturgical reform.

He had a share in writing *[Smectymnuus](/wiki/Smectymnuus "Smectymnuus")*, was appointed chaplain to the [Earl of Essex's regiment](/wiki/Earl_of_Essex%27s_regiment "Earl of Essex's regiment") in 1642, and a member of the [Westminster Assembly](/wiki/Westminster_Assembly "Westminster Assembly") in 1643. He represented the English Parliament in [Scotland](/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") in 1643, and attended the parliamentary commissions at the [Uxbridge Conference](/wiki/Uxbridge_Conference "Uxbridge Conference") in 1645. He was with Archbishop Laud before the latter's execution, and was chaplain to King [Charles I](/wiki/Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") at [Holmby House](/wiki/Holmby_House "Holmby House") and at [Carisbrooke Castle](/wiki/Carisbrooke_Castle "Carisbrooke Castle").

Later life
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Stephen_Marshall_(minister)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Later life")]

A moderate [Presbyterian](/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian"), he contributed to the [Westminster Shorter Catechism](/wiki/Westminster_Shorter_Catechism "Westminster Shorter Catechism") in 1647, and was one of the "Triers" in 1654. He died in November 1655 and was buried in [Westminster Abbey](/wiki/Westminster_Abbey "Westminster Abbey"), but his body was exhumed and maltreated at the [Restoration](/wiki/English_Restoration "English Restoration").
